af49a30e1f3fbab5: GEORGE TOWN: Tanjung Bungah residents have vowed to defend their coastal promontory — known as "Sore Thumb" — from destruction.
The community is mounting fierce resistance against plans to bulldoze the 22m-high headland and build a concrete retaining wall to make way for a five-storey private wellness centre.
The promontory took shape after rocks and earth were dumped into the sea from 2001, but the site was abandoned after stop-work orders halted illegal dumping.
Over the ensuing two decades, nature reclaimed the terrain, transforming the rocky mound into a self-regenerated coastal sanctuary inhabited by white-bellied sea eagles and dusky leaf monkeys.
Resident Oo Huei Ying said pushing retaining walls beyond the high-water mark would alter the seabed and trigger severe coastal erosion along the sensitive Tanjung Bungah coastline.

"A coastal park should co-exist with nature, not destroy it," she said, criticising blueprints that shave down the promontory for concrete tracks, parking bays, and amphitheatre-style retaining walls.
"Extending a retaining wall into the sea threatens our fragile shoreline.
"We want a genuine public park, not an over-engineered concrete development built at the expense of our coastal environment."
Annelies Allain, 81, who has lived in the area for 27 years, said watching further development on the regenerated promontory was a betrayal of the community's trust.
"There was once only a clean, open beach here where we could walk straight to the nearby Penang Swimming Club. Nature took over and the trees grew back naturally.
"Now they want to flatten it all just to secure sea views and commercial facilities for a private development. It is an injustice."
Another resident Dennis Au, in his 60s, echoed the call for preservation, urging authorities to abandon heavy construction on the public foreshore.
"The state's duty is to protect ecological balance, not shave away public hills for commercial gains.
"We will fight every inch."
For resident Jeya Shah, 59, the community's demands are uncompromising.
"Our demands are non-negotiable: any retaining wall must stay within the developer's private lot boundary. The promontory cannot be shaved down and the natural beach must be kept intact.
"The state government promised this would be gazetted as an open green lung with walking trails."
Tanjung Bungah residents have put forward their own low-impact, architect-designed master plan to transform the "Sore Thumb" into a nature park.
The community's counter-proposal directly challenges the state-approved plans.
Its 78-page master plan advocates retaining the hill's natural topography, preserving its tree cover and creating an eco-park modelled on the Penang Youth Park and the Moon Gate trails.
The community's plan also eliminates the need to bulldoze hillside slopes for car parks.
"Our plan costs the state nothing. The residents are ready to carry out gotong-royong and crowdfund the trail work ourselves, exactly as we have done over the years," Oo said.
"The only thing the state needs to do is leave the headland intact and ensure the developer's retaining walls remain inside their own boundary."

3891fd5c48e6a444: KUALA LUMPUR: The selection of Turkiye's Roketsan Atmaca antiship missile system to replace the cancelled Naval Strike Missile (NSM) on the Royal Malaysian Navy's littoral combat ships (LCS) could improve logistical efficiency and strengthen the country's defence industry.

Universiti Pertahanan Nasional Malaysia Centre for Defence and International Security Studies director Professor Dr Adam Leong said Atmaca was an excellent choice for the LCS, particularly as the same missile system would also equip the littoral mission ship batch 2 (LMS B2) vessels.
"The missile is competitive with other systems in the market, with the ability to engage surface vessels and fixed land targets at ranges exceeding 200km.

"It also features multiple guidance systems and counter-electronic warfare capabilities, while its land-based variant could reportedly be launched from coastal defence positions at ranges of up to 400km."
The Defence Ministry selected the Atmaca after evaluating proposals from Turkiye, France and Italy. Negotiations with the Turkish side are set to begin.
Minister Datuk Seri Mohamed Khaled Nordin said the 250km-range missile could be delivered as early as 2029, partly by leveraging Malaysia's existing Atmaca procurement for its LMS B2 vessels.
Leong said using a common missile system across different naval platforms would improve supply chain management, training, maintenance and logistical support.

"This added flexibility will provide additional options to strengthen the armed forces' joint-force capabilities by streamlining anti-ship, coastal-defence and land-attack missile requirements in the future."
He said the Atmaca was likely selected after the navy assessed its cost-effectiveness, delivery timeline and ease of integration with the LCS combat management system.

Janes Defence consultancy principal defence analyst Ridzwan Rahmat said the Atmaca offered Malaysia a viable alternative for meeting the immediate operational requirements of the LCS programme, although it had a shorter publicly documented testing record than the NSM.
The NSM, developed by Norwegian defence company Kongsberg Defence & Aerospace, was initially selected to arm the six LCS vessels under a 128.7 million euros contract signed in 2018.
However, Norway suspended the export licences for the missiles and associated launchers on Feb 4, 2026, before permanently revoking them on April 20.
Malaysia had paid 129.8 million euros, or about 94 per cent of the combined 137.91 million euros procurement value, according Khaled.
The missile systems had been manufactured, tested by the navy and were ready for delivery. Malaysia is seeking to recover the payments and claim compensation over the failed procurement.
On the Atmaca's integration, Ridzwan said adjustments would be required to the LCS combat systems, but the process should not be overly complicated.
"Turkish weapon systems were generally designed to be system-agnostic, allowing them to interface with radars, sensors and combat management systems from different manufacturers and countries.
"This would mean that the Atmaca could interface with the LCS's Thales SETIS combat management system, SMART-S search radar and TMEO Mk2 electro-optical tracking system," he said.
Ridzwan said the selection was also expected, given that the Atmaca would already be operated on the navy's LMS B2 ships.
He said the missile was in the same weight class as the NSM, meaning there would not be a need to rebalance the LCS's upper hull structure.
Using a common missile system across the LCS and LMS B2 fleets would also make logistical sense, potentially reducing costs and easing supply chain challenges, he said.
However, he said the missile's performance in Malaysia's hot and humid climate would need to be established.
"The Atmaca was developed by Turkiye in a much milder climate and it has largely not been proven out in the tropical region."

On potential technology transfer, Ridzwan said Turkiye had established a reputation for transferring defence technologies, adding that the benefits Malaysia could gain would depend on the readiness of the local industry.
"I think it is more a question of how ready the Malaysian defence industry is to receive that level of technology transfers."

651c3a08b38b2de4: Welcome to "The Sunday Spill: Weekly Beats", highlighting the top entertainment stories of the week so far.
Fazley Yaakob proposes to Datuk Seri Vida with custom ring, 1,200 drones

Singer and celebrity chef Datuk Fazley Yaakob surprised entrepreneur Datuk Seri Vida with a marriage proposal during a live concert in Kuala Lumpur, presenting her with a RM7,000 tiara-shaped ring alongside a 1,200-drone light display.
An emotional Vida accepted the proposal on the spot, putting to rest public speculation over whether their romance was merely a publicity stunt.
Tamil singer Zubir Khan treated like royalty at Pahang Deepavali celebrations

Tamil singer and composer Zubir Khan enjoyed his first Deepavali as a married man in Pahang, experiencing the traditional Thala Deepavali custom where newlyweds are treated like royalty and served special dishes on banana leaves.

Alongside his wife, Dr Heama Maleini, the 26-year-old artiste spent the festive period decorating their home, visiting family open houses, and gaining a deeper appreciation for Indian cultural traditions.
Chow Yun Fat, 71, sparks safety concerns after jogging on Hong Kong road

Hong Kong screen legend Chow Yun Fat prompted safety concerns online after a netizen spotted the 71-year-old fitness enthusiast jogging directly on a roadway near the Central and Western District Promenade rather than on a pedestrian pavement.
While several commenters warned of the hazards of running alongside moving traffic, supporters defended the actor by noting that Hong Kong runners often have limited path options.
Repairs wipe out earnings: Veteran singer Zaiton Sameon seeks car donation
Veteran songstress Zaiton Sameon is appealing for a vehicle donation after recurring mechanical breakdowns to her adopted daughter's ageing car consumed her modest performance earnings.
Left reliant on costly e-hailing rides to travel for sporadic out-of-state gigs, the 70-year-old singer is struggling financially to make ends meet.
Fireworks, vows: Christy Chung, 56, and Shawn Zhang mark 10th anniversary in Shenzhen

Actress Christy Chung , 56, and actor Shawn Zhang, 44, celebrated their 10th wedding anniversary with a romantic seaside vow-renewal ceremony and fireworks display in Shenzhen, joined by Chung's two younger daughters.
The milestone event celebrated a decade of marriage that has successfully weathered early public scrutiny over their 12-year age gap and career dynamics.
'36 is ideal': Grace Chan jokes she married Kevin Cheng too young at 27
Hong Kong actress Grace Chan , 35, admitted she occasionally lives vicariously through her single friends after marrying actor Kevin Cheng at the relatively young age of 27.
During a recent interview, the mother of three praised Hong Kong men for being attentive partners whilst jokingly advising her 29-year-old host to wait until 36 to settle down.

52c53cf2eb98df59: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 15 — Barisan Nasional (BN) and Perikatan Nasional (PN) captured 24 of Melaka’s 28 seats in yesterday’s state election, marking the third state poll in four months where Pakatan Harapan (PH) has lost ground after Johor and Negeri Sembilan.
Here are three takeaways from the result.
BN-PAS formula delivers again
Melaka is the second consecutive state election, following Negeri Sembilan, in which BN and PN jointly outperformed PH.
Their combined tally of 24 seats edges out the 23 they won separately in 2021.

Before polling day, analysts noted that the arrangement could consolidate Malay votes, ending the vote-splitting among Umno, PAS, and Bersatu since 2018 that previously allowed PH to win multi-cornered fights.
This outcome strengthens the case for a formal BN-PN partnership heading into the 16th general election (GE16).
Still, caveats remain: parliamentary seats are larger and more diverse than state constituencies, while BN and PAS must still navigate overlapping ambitions and competing leadership interests.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Pakatan Harapan (PH) candidate for the Bukit Katil state seat Adly Zahari and PKR communications director Adam Adli hold a press conference at the PH main operations room in Melaka on November 14, 2026. — Bernama pic
Growing pressure for early GE16
Last night’s result gives BN more momentum to press for an early GE16. The call was already being made before polling day.

Umno president Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, who is also deputy prime minister, said in Melaka on November 10 that it would be better to return the mandate to the people than to carry out a Cabinet reshuffle after DAP secretary-general Anthony Loke resigned as transport minister.

Analysts previously said BN and PAS are keen to capitalise on the momentum from the Negeri Sembilan, Johor and Melaka elections by pushing for an early general election. One analyst said earlier that Umno has every incentive to force an early GE16 because it thinks it is unbeatable with PAS’s support.

PH has pushed back. DAP chairman Gobind Singh Deo said BN leaders who have lost confidence in Anwar should resign from the Cabinet rather than push for dissolution, while Loke said Anwar still has a mandate and sufficient support in Parliament to continue governing.
Anwar has said the timing of GE16 depends on several factors and that any dissolution would be decided after consulting coalition partners and the Yang di-Pertuan Agong.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu) vice-president and Melaka state leadership body chairman Datuk Mohd Radzi Md Jidin (fifth from left) with the party’s eight candidates at the Bersatu candidate announcement ceremony for the 16th Melaka State Election at Baitul Tariq, Klebang, October 29, 2026. — Bernama pic
Third forces are shut out

Contesting seven seats under its own logo after falling out with PAS, Bersatu won none. The wipeout carries clear ramifications going into GE16, with PH exploring a partnership with Bersatu to counter the BN-PN cooperation.
Parti Bersama Malaysia fared no better, failing to win any of the 16 seats it contested.

Before the Melaka poll, analysts said Bersatu faced the toughest strategic crossroads, weighing reconciliation with PAS, negotiations with PH, or leading a smaller bloc of parties excluded from the BN-PN arrangement.
Every seat that went against BN fell either to PH’s urban bastions or PAS-linked PN candidates, shutting out newcomers and minor contenders.

a780f508dc3762d1: PARIS, Nov 15 — Lethal autonomous weapons powered by artificial intelligence are set to revolutionise warfare but there is no proper regulatory or legal framework governing the new technology.
A conference starting Monday at the United Nations in Geneva will discuss how to establish curbs and prohibitions on such weapons, called killer robots by some.
But some analysts doubt the discussions at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) will keep pace with the fast-changing weapons.
AFP looks at three key questions ahead of the conference.
What are LAWS?

Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) “can identify, select, and engage a target without the intervention of a human operator in the execution of these tasks,” said Jean-Marc Rickli, head of global and emerging risks at the Geneva Centre for Security Policy.

Autonomous weapons have long existed. An anti-personnel mine “is an autonomous weapon in the sense that it explodes when someone steps on it,” said Laure de Roucy-Rochegonde of the Centre for Geopolitics of Technology at the French Institute of International Relations (IFRI).

But with the proliferation of AI-enhanced drones, such weapons are now “capable of selecting and engaging a target that was not predetermined, adapting to their environment without human intervention,” said Rickli.
So the critical issue for potential regulators lies in determining the level of human control over the decision to employ such a weapon.
The United States refers to an “appropriate levels of human judgement” in the use of autonomous weapons.
France maintains that a human must remain in the decision-making loop and bans “lethal autonomous weapons systems” (LAWS) but permits “partially autonomous” systems known as PLAWS.

“The human role is always ensured through what is termed ‘appropriate control’ by a military commander – a concept that varies in scope depending on the system’s criticality and the operational context,” said Rear Admiral Vincent Sebastien, deputy director of the French defence ministry’s Agency for Defence Artificial Intelligence (AMIAD).
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Bavaria’s State Premier Markus Soeder (second left) and German Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche (third left) receive a briefing in front of a KNDS Dingo drone-defence vehicle equipped with Tytan drones during the opening of TYTAN Technologies’ new production facility for autonomous interceptor drones in Munich on November 9, 2026. — AFP pic
The ethical issues?

“We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: the autonomous targeting of humans by machines,” UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, and International Committee of the Red Cross president Mirjana Spoljaric warned in a joint statement in August.
But analysts said the Geneva discussions, while important, will touch only part of the issue.
Today, the diminishing role of humans is being driven by the growing use of AI in analysis and targeting.
Rickli said the scope of the agenda in Geneva is “very narrow”.
“It fails to encompass the full range of issues surrounding AI on the battlefield” – an area where its use is expanding, particularly in target generation.
He said this was seen in the US-Israeli war against Iran this year “where the Americans engaged as many as 1,000 targets per day” inside Iran.

“There are a host of problems and unacceptable risks associated with targeting and decision-support systems,” added de Roucy-Rochegonde. “Part of this debate concerns systems that are already widely deployed on the battlefield.”

“What kind of human supervision is required to ensure that the operator is genuinely exercising their own judgement rather than simply providing a rubber stamp for the machine’s recommendations?” she asked.
How quickly is the situation changing?

The autonomous weapons to be discussed in Geneva are not yet in widespread use, although analysts have noted that they have been deployed by Russia in its invasion of Ukraine as well as US attacks in Iran.
But the spread is inevitable.
“Autonomy will very quickly become a reality on the battlefield,” warned rear admiral Sebastien.
“Autonomous weapon systems are not part of a distant future – a race towards greater autonomy in weapons systems is already well underway,” Guterres and Spoljaric said in their statement.

Yet significant doubts and dangers remain, Dario Amodei, head of the AI giant Anthropic, warned this year: “Today, frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.”
But ultimately, the incentive for major powers is too strong.
Swarms of autonomous drones – which “aim to neutralise an adversary through saturation” – would be highly effective, and some states view them as a crucial strategic advantage, said Rickli.
In January, the Chinese defence ministry described swarms of autonomous drones as the “new face of warfare.”

“In an era of sharp military competition, the first state to normalise fully autonomous lethal strikes will reset expectations for everyone else,” said Gerald Mako, a research affiliate of Cambridge University in the Small Wars Journal. — AFP
5281b6660facabce: LONDON, Nov 15 — Britain’s world-renowned entertainment sector is facing mounting calls to usher in sweeping reforms and greater oversight, amid a fresh slew of rape and sexual abuse allegations against some of its powerful male stars.

“The media industry will need to look at itself and ensure whether it is taking all of the steps needed to protect the safety of women and girls who work within the industry,” Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned late Thursday after days of torrid headlines.

Comedian and ex-Hollywood actor Russell Brand was on Monday jailed for over 10 years for rape and sexual assault against four women dating back to the 2000s, when he was at the height of his fame, including raping a fan and abusing female staff from media organisations where he worked.
And on Friday London’s Metropolitan Police said they were investigating allegations of “serious sexual offences” made against children’s author David Walliams.
The comic and bestselling writer has denied the accusations published this week in a joint Guardian and ITV news investigation.

Comedian Lucy Beaumont, who revealed she had been one of the Guardian’s “whistleblowers” after learning second-hand about the accusations, said she felt there “is a window of opportunity to change things”.
Frank conversations were being had in an industry which had “no HR department, no proper duty of care”, Beaumont told Sky News.

Culture Minister Lisa Nandy, who has said she believes such abuse still exists, will meet with industry bosses on Tuesday, and warned ministers “would not hesitate” to take action if protections put in place are inadequate.
‘Culture of doubt’
Experts agreed that society-wide solutions were needed alongside tighter government reforms of the legal system and workplace rules.
“What we really need is a cultural reckoning that fundamentally shifts how we respond to credible allegations of sexual harm,” University of Leeds media lecturer Kat Higgins argued.
She co-authored the 2023 book “Believability: Sexual Violence, Media, and the Politics of Doubt”.
“The more difficult challenge is to dismantle the culture of doubt that confronts survivors when they do speak out,” she said.
Higgins also called for a reform of the legal system to stop the “pernicious use” of non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) to “silence survivors”.
Walliams was initially able to block the publication of the claims against him, with his legal team arguing he was “highly likely” to die by suicide if they were aired.
“Such men should not be able to use their wealth or the law to coerce women and girls into silence and to shield themselves from justice,” Higgins said.
Sex abuse and harassment scandals over decades have rocked Britain’s entertainment industry since the 2012 shock discovery that children’s TV presenter Jimmy Savile was a prolific offender.
The revelation that Savile, who died in 2011, used his celebrity status to sexually abuse dozens of children rocked the country and sparked a wider police probe.

Others whose offences have emerged included 1970s glam rocker Gary Glitter and Australian-born artist and musician Rolf Harris, once one of the UK’s best-loved entertainers before being convicted in 2014 of underage-sex crimes.
The #MeToo movement that began in 2017 also brought renewed focus on sexual crimes and harassment within the industry.
‘Perfect storm’
The culture has improved but “far too slowly,” said expert Anna Bull of the University of York, as fresh allegations emerged in the Times on Friday that six more women had been assaulted by Brand.
Bull has been studying sexual harassment in UK organisations for a decade, and was lead author of a 2023 report warning that the film and TV industry was still failing to tackle sexual harassment.
“Attitudes have changed, what becomes appropriate has changed,” she said, but “the systems and the regulatory oversight has not shifted sufficiently”.
Tougher legislation requiring employers to take all reasonable steps to prevent sexual harassment only came into force a few weeks ago, she pointed out.
Even Beaumont, who is an established UK comedian, admitted she was terrified she might “never work in telly again” after speaking out.

Those working in film and TV, many of them young freelancers, are particularly vulnerable due to their precarious employment status, gender imbalances in power structures and a “massive downturn” in job vacancies in recent years, Bull said.
“So we’ve got a perfect storm where people don’t want to make formal reports or don’t want to raise concerns at all,” she said. — AFP
43f9e2a79705a30c: YANGON, Nov 15 — Myanmar faces a pivotal week as neighbouring nations weigh the future of post-coup relations, while the United Nations’ top court threatens a verdict of genocide over its dark past.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is scheduled on Thursday to rule whether Myanmar committed genocide against its marginalised Muslim Rohingya minority.
The case looms over a three-day meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) due to debate its policy freezing Myanmar out of summits since a 2021 putsch.
Rohingya activists say the pending judgement should haunt the minds of Asean leaders when they meet in the Philippines starting Sunday.

“We are waiting to see what the outcome will be on that day, the judgement for everything we have been experiencing for generations,” said a 25-year-old Yangon-based Rohingya activist who requested anonymity for security reasons.
“If they welcome people who lack basic humanity and destroyed our lives, our futures and our possessions, we will be very let down,” he added.
Man in question
The UN court case and Asean’s diplomatic dilemma are separate issues on paper. But both converge on one man: Min Aung Hlaing.
The 11-nation Asean bloc has shunned Myanmar leaders from summits since his military coup turfed out the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and sparked civil war.
The Hague case dates back to 2017, when Myanmar is accused of breaching the United Nations Genocide Convention by brutalising the Rohingya.
The judgement due Thursday will weigh state culpability, not individual guilt.
But Min Aung Hlaing led the military as it spearheaded the mass killings, rape and arson targeting the Rohingya and driving nearly 750,000 into Bangladesh as refugees.
This April, he was installed as president after elections rejected by democracy watchdogs, and is waging a charm offensive seeking acceptance in the diplomatic fold.
“If the ICJ finds that Myanmar committed genocide, it would seriously weaken Min Aung Hlaing’s efforts,” said Wai Yan Phyo Naing, visiting scholar at Taiwan’s Academia Sinica.
“Any public association with him could create political and reputational risks, especially for governments that claim to support human rights and international law.”
Signs of support
But Myanmar has already secured signals of support to return to Asean.
As civilian president, Min Aung Hlaing has had red-carpet welcomes in bloc members Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam.
Even Muslim-majority Malaysia hosted him last month, albeit to expedite the return of thousands of Myanmar migrants as a wave of prejudice towards Rohingya refugees swept the nation.

Rights groups expressed alarm about the fate of those returned, but that did not prevent Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim promising “Malaysia will do whatever is possible” to smooth Myanmar’s normalisation in Asean.
Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the International Crisis Group, said the ICJ ruling may have little impact on Min Aung Hlaing’s momentum.
“Governments willing to host him are unlikely to change course over a ruling addressed to the Myanmar state, which places no legal restriction on him personally,” he said.
“It may make some members more cautious about being seen to move quickly, but I doubt it will stop the drift towards normalisation.”
Diplomatic drift
Some analysts argue that a finding Myanmar committed genocide may actually embolden Min Aung Hlaing, confirming he can rub shoulders with world leaders regardless.
It may also stoke division between Asean nations arguing he should be ostracised and those favouring engagement to coax Myanmar towards a different future.
Post-coup Myanmar has been represented by senior civil servants at Asean summits, an arrangement which will remain in place for the Manila meeting.
The bloc’s rotating chair will at the end of this year pass from the Philippines to Singapore, a city-state analysts say opposes normalising Myanmar ties.
But in 2028, it will be the turn of Thailand, which shares a long border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations.
Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said Thursday he did not forsee the ICJ ruling would disrupt the process of “calibrated re-engagement”.
“Asean is unlikely to fully embrace Min Aung Hlaing at a summit level soon,” said independent Myanmar analyst David Mathieson.
“But it’s only a matter of time.” — AFP
b03274b006634f8e: STARBASE: Elon Musk's SpaceX on Saturday carried out the first-ever recovery of a spaceship, pulling off a successful "catch" of its Starship vessel as it returned to its launch site after a day in orbit.

The spaceship emerged from a cloudy sky after withstanding the extreme heat of re-entering the Earth's atmosphere, and descended slowly over Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical "chopstick arms" above Launch Pad 2.
The feat marked a milestone in the space industry's decades-long pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems – a goal that can drastically reduce mission costs and make more frequent launches possible.
"That was the Holy Grail of space flight, plummeting through fire to be snatched out of the air by steel. We caught a Starship and now, everything changes," SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot said.

Crowds gathered on the Gulf of Mexico beach near Starbase broke into cheers as the spaceship eased into its high-tech nest on the 15th test flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket system.

This time the Starship spacecraft that gives the rocket system its name orbited Earth 14 times and deployed 26 satellites for Musk's Starlink satellite internet constellation during its 22-hour journey.

Until now SpaceX had captured returning booster rockets three times. However, the "catch" of Starship was extraordinarily complex because the spaceship fell much faster and from a much higher altitude than boosters do.

Clayton Swope, an aerospace expert at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, called the mission a "huge technical achievement and proves the whole idea of Starship as a fully reusable spaceship can work."
"Let's see how quickly they can do it again," he added.
- 'GIANT SWOOSH' -
The vessel's path home was carefully mapped out by engineers.

"If you want to get back to the east coast of Texas, you have to fly over the entire continent to get back there. So inevitably, you're flying over land and we spend a lot of time figuring out the safest way to do that," senior SpaceX engineer Lars Blackmore said.

Starship flew over sparsely inhabited desert areas, wove over towns and then carried out a "giant swoosh manoeuvre" in its final approach, looping around the cities of Texas' Rio Grande Valley and approaching its landing site from the east.
Some versions of Starship are designed to launch internet satellites and data centres into orbit, while other iterations will be made to ferry people to the Moon and Mars.
US space agency NASA is expecting Starship to serve as a lunar lander on its Artemis mission. On Saturday, Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated Musk and SpaceX.
"It was almost magic... Making more believers by the day... one step closer to (the Moon)," he said on X.
- REFUELING CHALLENGE -

Musk, the world's richest person, has already revolutionised the space sector with the partially reusable Falcon rockets, which regularly launch satellites and carry astronauts to the International Space Station.

But the Starship project has been plagued by delays as SpaceX grapples with novel engineering challenges, including the unsolved problem of transferring fuel to the spaceship while in orbit – a requirement for any journey to the Moon or Mars.

It will also need to further fine-tune the Super Heavy booster, which ran into a technical issue Friday on its descent, forcing a diversion to the Gulf of Mexico just off the launch site. It, too, was supposed to have been caught by the "chopstick arms."
The booster automatically self-destructed – a fireball erupting from the booster – before hitting the water.
Following SpaceX's high-profile stock market debut in June that raised about US$85.7 billion, the company is investing heavily in production and launch capabilities.

During a tour of its million-square-foot factory at Starbase on Friday, SpaceX officials told journalists it now has the capability to produce a spaceship every two weeks and a booster every four weeks.--AFP

a1bdfc908d130274: PARIS: Tens of thousands of protesters paraded in the streets of France on Saturday, some clambering up statues with French flags as they vented on issues ranging from the rising cost of living to a proposal to give police greater legal protection.

77df959fb47c40ea: BANGKOK: A teenage pop star from the Philippines won the first Asia edition of Eurovision on Saturday after a night of power ballads, pop-dance hits and pyrotechnics from the makers of the cult European kitsch fest.

Hosts Thailand finished a close second, followed by Vietnam, Malaysia and Laos, with Nepal, Cambodia and Bangladesh languishing at the bottom of the points table.

Eleven countries had joined the competition that organisers hope will start a new chapter for Eurovision, a cultural phenomenon in Europe for its lavish outfits, soaring vocals -- and sometimes tricky geopolitics.

Eurovision is the world's biggest televised live music event, drawing 131 million viewers in 2026, and over the past 70 years has helped to launch the careers of global superstars such as ABBA and Celine Dion.
But the big question is whether it can take off in Asia, the world's most populous region with more than enough music shows of its own.

"I'm very pleased it's come to Asia. We've been waiting so long!" said Malaysian mega-fan Fauzan, 37, one of the first in line for the show.

Spectacular staging is a hallmark of Eurovision but budgets were tight in Bangkok, so most performers relied on smoke, flares and eye-catching visuals.
There were deeply heartfelt performances but also a lot of fun, including the use of multi-coloured tuk-tuks -- the symbol of Bangkok -- to ferry contestants on stage.
Singing must be live under Eurovision rules and some of the performers struggled, but the producers ramped up the energy, with a pop track by Vietnam's Toc Tien morphing into a heavy dance tune.
The Asia edition was organised by commercial television -- unlike Eurovision, which is run by national broadcasters -- and the contestants were mostly well known in their home countries.

7a98f561f849cd66: AI could help bridge educational inequality in a country where thousands of students still learn outdoors
Originally published on Global Voices
Photo taken by Rahul Ingle, May 2012. This file is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

In many communities across Mozambique, formal education still takes place in the open air, under trees, in improvised yards, or inside fragile structures that barely offer protection from the sun and rain. These so-called outdoor classrooms are not an innovative pedagogical choice, but more often than not, the expression of a structural deficiency: a lack of infrastructure, a shortage of materials, and an estimated deficit of around 12,000 teachers in 2025.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->During the rainy season (roughly November to March in Mozambique), the situation becomes more challenging. In several regions, the school calendar must be adjusted to respond to inclement weather, such as heavy rains that disrupt classes and hinder the continuity of teaching between November and March each year.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->In this context, the question arises: What is the place of artificial intelligence (AI) in an educational system that, in many areas of the country, is still fighting for the basics?<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
A school without walls

In rural districts of provinces like Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Zambézia, it is common to find classes of students studying under trees. The Minister of Education, Samaria Tovela, has been evaluating schedule adjustments because, while classes are frequently interrupted during the rainy season, concentration becomes a constant challenge during periods of intense heat. Without proper blackboards or textbooks, and often with a single teacher responsible for several classes, the learning process becomes irregular and deeply unequal when one million students learn to read and write on the ground.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->This scenario highlights a central problem: Learning depends on minimum standards that are not yet guaranteed in Mozambique. At the same time, one of the biggest obstacles to introducing technologies like AI in rural African contexts is the lack of connectivity. In Mozambique, about 73 percent of the population lacks internet access, according to 2024 data from the Ministry of Transport and Communications.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->Regional inequalities limit these initiatives, despite some progress recorded in recent years. This limitation directly affects the potential of solutions such as distance learning or digital learning platforms.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
Language, culture, and the role of the state<!--TgQPHd|||[[2,[null,null,1,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,null,[351768,null,0]],[],null,1]]-->

Another critical challenge is the linguistic and cultural dimension. In Africa, where more than 2,000 languages are spoken, only a fraction — around 49 — are represented on digital platforms like Google’s translation service. Integrating Mozambique’s Indigenous languages, such as Emakhuwa, Xichangana, or Elomwe, into digital educational tools could significantly increase students’ comprehension and engagement, especially in the early years of schooling. However, implementing these solutions raises practical questions in contexts where access to technology is still limited.

<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->The overwhelming majority of the Mozambican population speaks a Bantu language most frequently at home (81.7 percent), and a portion cannot speak Portuguese at all (41.9 percent), though it is the sole official language of the country due to its colonial history. Despite this, the media, official government communications, and healthcare institutions continue to privilege Portuguese to the detriment of Bantu languages — the languages of the masses — which, activists argue, constitutes a form of social exclusion. Emerging initiatives, however, show that it is possible to bridge this gap with the aid of technology. In Johannesburg, for instance, tech startups are developing AI solutions tailored to African languages.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->
Risks and potential

Offline tools, pre-loaded content, and digital pedagogical assistants are some of the possible solutions to address the deficiencies and limitations of Mozambique’s education system. While the government does not yet have specific policies to integrate AI tools in schools, advocates say the state could play a central role in integrating technology into the daily lives of students and teachers. This also involves investing in teacher training; ensuring basic infrastructure; facilitating energy access; and strengthening partnerships with universities, startups, and international organizations.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

Talking about artificial intelligence in outdoor classrooms may seem contradictory at first glance, but it is precisely in these contexts that technology needs to be considered creatively and responsibly, not as a replacement for the essential, but as a strategic complement.

The priority remains clear: Building schools, training teachers, and ensuring access to basic materials. The question is how to integrate developed technology without creating profound inequalities, respecting local contexts, and placing the student and teacher at the center of decision-making. In a country where learning still takes place under trees, the future of education will depend not only on the technology available, but also on the political and social choices that define who has access to knowledge and under what conditions.
Written (Português) by Tirso Sitoe
Translated (English) by Masudul Zarif

0bcb2422f753d22d: KUALA LUMPUR: Pakatan Harapan candidate Kerk Chee Yee, 34, emerged as the youngest winner in the 16th Melaka election, while Chief Minister-elect Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh, 65, was the oldest.

Kerk polled 14,078 votes in a four-cornered contest for the Ayer Keroh state seat, defeating Perikatan Nasional candidate Gan Peng Lam (8,474 votes), Muhammad Muhaimin Lau Abdullah of Bersama (1,932 votes) and Mohd Hamnaim Mohamad of Bersatu (1,077 votes).
Kerk, who has held the seat for two terms, won with a majority of 5,604 votes.
Ayer Keroh, which has 38,252 registered voters, is one of four state constituencies under the Hang Tuah Jaya parliamentary constituency.
Meanwhile, Rauf retained the Tanjung Bidara seat after securing 10,079 votes to defeat PH candidate Mohd Yunazri Mustamiri, who received 1,464 votes in a straight fight.
The Melaka Barisan Narional chairman won with a majority of 8,615 votes, up from 364 in the 2021 state election.
Meanwhile, only four of the 14 women candidates who contested the election won their seats, comprising three from BN and one from PH.
The BN winners were Tuminah Kadi @ Mohd Hashim in Pantai Kundor, Siti Aisyah Mahmood in Pengkalan Batu and Khaidhirah Abu Zahar in Rim.
Tuminah defeated Bersatu candidate Asmah Samat with a majority of 2,752 votes, polling 8,864 against her rival's 6,112.
Siti Aisyah, the sole female candidate in Pengkalan Batu, won a four-cornered contest with a majority of 6,358 votes.
She defeated PH's Jason Tze-xi Nathan (5,478 votes), Bersatu's Norhizam Hassan Baktee (876 votes) and Bersama's Goh Han Koon (618 votes).
Rim incumbent Khaidhirah polled 9,847 votes to defeat PH's Esma Eazreen Husin, who received 2,757 votes, with a majority of 7,090.
PH candidate Leng Chau Yen retained the Bandar Hilir seat after polling 9,942 votes, defeating BN's Lok Huey Yee (2,085 votes) and Mohd Nor Rashidi Ab. Jalil (1,315 votes) with a majority of 7,857.
BN won 21 of the 28 seats in the election to secure a two-thirds majority, while PH retained four seats and PN won three.
8655cdba79c50582: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian vocal powerhouse Aina Abdul has flown the national flag high on the regional stage, securing a commendable fourth-place finish at the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 in Bangkok, Thailand, last night.
Performing as the 11th and final act of the evening at the One Bangkok Forum, Aina dazzled the crowd with her self-penned power ballad, Bluest Sky.
She scored 82 points from the professional jury and 70 points from the public vote, finishing with a respectable total of 152 points.
The Philippines' Carmelle clinched the coveted crown with 211 points following an energetic rendition of Sobra-Sobra.
The trophy was presented by Eurovision Song Contest 2026 winner Dara of Bulgaria.
Meanwhile, Thailand's Mang x Daou finished second with 170 points for Aroma, and Vietnam's Tóc Tiên placed third with 164 points for Em Tiên.

Despite stiff competition from 11 participating nations—including South Korea, Cambodia, Laos, Mongolia, Bhutan, Bangladesh, and Nepal—Aina's stirring performance drew roaring applause from the audience. Arranged by legendary Malaysian musician Mac Chew, Bluest Sky was inspired by Aina's pet cat, Hiro, and explores themes of deep, overwhelming love that is hard to let go of.

Visually, the staging was a triumph. Dressed in a striking, ethereal gown by longtime collaborator Melinda Looi—featuring shimmering white, turquoise blue, and translucent tones—Aina brought a water-themed concept to life. Supported by a giant water-droplet prop and dramatic LED visuals, the stage transformed from a single droplet into surging waves, mirroring the song's emotional build-up.

"When I found out Eurovision was finally coming to Asia, I immediately wanted to perform. I am overjoyed that this dream has come true," said Aina, who has followed the iconic contest since her idol Céline Dion competed. "As for my dress, it's once again something magical, and I always know that Melinda works wonders."

Having earned her spot to represent Malaysia after her standout win at the 40th Anugerah Juara Lagu (AJL40), Aina was cheered on by fans back home via live broadcasts on official broadcaster TV3 and the streaming platform Tonton.
Persatuan Karyawan Malaysia (Karyawan) president Datuk Freddie Fernandez praised Aina's world-class showing, noting that the top four acts put up a fierce fight.
"While she didn't win, we should all be proud of Aina for a commendable, world-class performance that set the benchmark really high for all Malaysian artistes," he said.
His views were shared by the five Malaysian jurors: chief juror AG Coco, Justin Seow, Iman Tang, Bobby Husaini, and Shamshul Azree Samshir.

During the three-hour spectacle—co-hosted by Thai television personalities Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop—the panel had accurately tipped Aina as a frontrunner, while predicting tough competition from the Philippines and Thailand.

3ecae36d88babf28: This week, I speak with Salim Ramji, Chief Executive Officer of Vanguard Group, one of the largest asset managers in the world. Founded by John Bogle in 1975 and owned by the funds it manages, and therefore by its clients, Vanguard hired Salim in July 2024 to succeed Tim Buckley, making him the first CEO recruited from outside the firm. He arrived after a decade at BlackRock, where he led its enormous iShares and index-investing business.

Salim began his career as a lawyer at Clifford Chance in London and Hong Kong, after earning a bachelor’s degree in economics and politics from the University of Toronto and a master’s degree in law from Cambridge. He left law for McKinsey, where he rose to senior partner and led the firm’s Asset & Wealth Management practice. In 2014, he moved to BlackRock as Head of Corporate Strategy, then ran U.S. Wealth Advisory, and ultimately became Global Head of iShares & Index Investing, overseeing the firm’s ETF and index business. He left BlackRock in January 2024, and Vanguard named him CEO that May.

We discuss his path from law to consulting to BlackRock, and what it means to be the first outsider to run a firm with Vanguard’s culture and ownership structure. We also talk about Vanguard’s acquisition of Altruist, the advisor-focused custody and technology platform, and what the deal signals about the future of financial advice. Salim last joined me on Masters in Business in August 2020, when he was running iShares at BlackRock.
Our previous conversation is here; A transcript of our conversation is available here this week.

You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, and Bloomberg. All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here.

Be sure to check out our Masters in Business next week with David Eichhorn, Chief Executive Officer and Head of Investment Strategies at NISA Investment Advisors, a 100% employee-owned asset manager based in Clayton, Missouri overseeing roughly $483 billion in assets.
ab1a2f9979e68047: KUALA LUMPUR: The Melaka election results reflect growing public support for Parti Wawasan Negara, with its president Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin describing the outcome as a clear call for a change in leadership and the country's direction.
Hamzah said the combined victory of Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional which secured 24 of the 28 seats contested, showed that voters wanted a change.
He described the outcome as a "people's referendum" and claimed that Pakatan Harapan and Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim had been rejected by voters.
He also pointed out that PKR and Amanah had lost all the seats they contested.
"This is not a political coincidence, but an increasingly clear pattern of public rejection. The reality is that PH is not the government of choice of the people," he said in a statement.
Hamzah said the trend had begun in Johor, continued in Negri Sembilan and was now reflected in Melaka.
He said Wawasan had strengthened its position as a national party with a Malaysian identity, adding that it had retained the Bemban state seat with a bigger majority.
The party had also put up a strong challenge in Kesidang, which he described as a DAP stronghold.
Hamzah said the results showed that inclusive politics based on values and a national agenda had a place among voters.
He cited the party's victories in Gemas, Klawang and Sikamat in the recent Negri Sembilan state election as further evidence of its growing support.

"The struggle does not end in Melaka. The Blue Wave will be strengthened, the New National Consensus will continue to be championed and, with the people's support, the next step is to bring change to Putrajaya," he said.

James Chin daripada University of Tasmania berkata, undi Melayu yang sebelum ini berpecah antara Umno dan PAS kini semakin disatukan melalui kerjasama mereka, sekali gus memberi kelebihan besar kepada kedua-dua parti di kerusi majoriti Melayu.
“Umno dan PAS hampir mustahil untuk dikalahkan di kawasan majoriti Melayu jika mereka bekerjasama,” katanya kepada FMT.
Chin berkata, kemenangan gabungan Barisan Nasional (BN) dan Perikatan Nasional (PN), yang ditunjangi Umno dan PAS, membuktikan kekuatan mereka secara bergabung dalam pilihan raya.
“Keputusan di Melaka tidak menunjukkan kebangkitan semula Umno dalam pilihan raya. Kejayaan Umno pada pilihan raya kini banyak bergantung kepada kerjasamanya dengan PAS,” katanya.
Chin berkata, 'tsunami Melayu' yang tercetus hasil kerjasama itu semakin jelas kelihatan dalam keputusan PRN di Johor, Negeri Sembilan dan kini Melaka.
“Selagi mereka mampu mengekalkan kerjasama ini, mereka pasti berada dalam kedudukan yang kukuh untuk menang PRU16,” katanya.
PRU16 perlu diadakan selewat-lewatnya pada awal 2028, namun ramai menjangkakan ia mungkin berlangsung tahun depan.
Pada PRN Melaka hari ini, gabungan BN-PN memenangi 24 daripada 28 kerusi untuk memperoleh majoriti besar di DUN.
BN bertanding di 23 kerusi, manakala PAS, Wawasan dan Gerakan daripada PN meletakkan calon di baki lima kerusi lagi, dengan semua parti bersetuju untuk tidak bersaing di kerusi sama.
Pada PRN 2021, BN memperoleh majoriti dua pertiga selepas memenangi 21 kerusi, walaupun seorang Adun Umno kemudiannya melompat ke PAS.

c6292072bffc5139: PETALING JAYA: Barisan Nasional (BN) dan Perikatan Nasional (PN) secara rasmi memenangi 24 daripada 28 DUN pada PRN Melaka ke-16, sekali gus memperoleh majoriti lebih dua pertiga untuk membentuk kerajaan negeri.

a981bc397b0d981d: PETALING JAYA: Umno’s electoral fortunes now depend largely on teaming up with PAS, a political analyst said today, pointing out that the Melaka election results did not indicate an Umno revival.

James Chin of the University of Tasmania said Malay votes, historically divided between Umno and PAS, were now being consolidated through their cooperation, giving the two parties a significant advantage in Malay-majority seats.
"Umno and PAS are virtually unbeatable in Malay-majority areas if they work together,” he told FMT.
The victory of the alliance between Barisan Nasional (BN) and Perikatan Nasional (PN), in which Umno and PAS are the lynchpins, was a demonstration of their combined electoral strength, Chin said.
“The Melaka results do not indicate a revival of Umno’s electoral fortunes. Umno’s electoral fortunes now depend largely on teaming up with PAS,” he said.
Chin said the “Malay tsunami” brought about by their cooperation had become increasingly evident in the election results in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and now Melaka.
“As long as they can sustain this cooperation, they will certainly be in a strong position to win the 16th general election,” he said.
The next national election is due by early 2028 at the latest, but is widely speculated to be held next year.
In the Melaka election today, the BN-PN alliance won 24 of the 28 seats for a supermajority in the state assembly.
BN contested 23 seats, while PAS, Wawasan and Gerakan of PN fielded candidates in the remaining five seats, with all parties agreeing not to contest against one another.
In the 2021 state election, BN secured a two-thirds majority after winning 21 seats, although an Umno assemblyman later defected to PAS.
Chin said the BN-PN cooperation could strengthen Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s political ambitions. He said Zahid was positioning himself to become the next prime minister after GE16.

Political analyst Azmi Hassan of Akademi Nusantara said the Melaka victory would also give Zahid, who is deputy prime minister, greater confidence to distance Umno from Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Pakatan Harapan.
While seat negotiations for the general election could prove difficult, both Umno and PAS recognised their mutual importance, he said.
“If BN contested on its own, Johor would remain its stronghold. However, the results in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka would have been quite different if BN had gone solo,” he said.

Azmi said PAS currently holds more parliamentary seats than Umno and is also more dominant in states such as Perak and Pahang. “Nevertheless, both PAS and Umno need each other, and they understand that.”
c86f5497853424ba: MILAN: Italian regulators fined Facebook parent company Meta €805 million (US$880 million) for accessing users' photos without their "specific" consent, the country's data protection authority said on Saturday.

Through the Facebook application for Android devices, Meta accessed photographs, videos and related metadata belonging to Italian users "without obtaining specific consent and without properly informing them", the authority said in a statement.

In late October, authorities in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion for having misled the state's residents for more than a decade over use of their data – a record fine for the company, which slammed it as a "tax" on freedom of expression.
Saturday's latest fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a tech giant.
In 2021, Amazon received more than €1.1 billion fine for breaching competition law.
That sum was subsequently reduced to €752 million on appeal.
Meta may also appeal the latest fine. When contacted, the US group had not responded by Saturday afternoon.
The penalty imposed on Facebook relates to its gallery suggestions feature, available since 2023, which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts as they are browsing.

According to Italy's regulator, Facebook requested access to the gallery via a single authorisation valid for the entire app, preceded by a generic notice requesting enabling of other features, which did not allow users to understand that they were also authorising suggestions from their gallery.

Meta will now notably have to seek consent by means of a separate and specific request for the feature concerned and clearly signpost what it is used for, namely that it involves access to a user's photo gallery, as well as how to disable it.

In determining the size of the fine, the authority said it took into account "the high number of people affected" – around 20 million Android users in Italy – and the duration of the infringement, "which is still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".
The authority also cited "Meta's lack of cooperation during the investigation".
It imposed a fine amounting to roughly 0.4% of the group's annual turnover, which hit US$201 billion in 2025, for a net profit of US$60.5 billion.

9a0f369b15afb410: PETALING JAYA: The government has approved a 99-year lease renewal for the Kuala Lumpur and Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall (KLSCAH).
The land premium has been fixed at a nominal RM1,000, a significant reduction from the earlier estimated premium of nearly RM4.67 million, Bernama reported.

Federal territories minister Hannah Yeoh, in a Facebook post today, said the decision reflected the government's commitment to safeguard Kuala Lumpur's historical landmarks and ensure institutions of heritage significance can continue to serve future generations.

She said the nominal premium was approved following Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's commitment to give special consideration to the preservation of the historical building, after visiting the hall during a Chinese New Year celebration on Feb 17.
Hannah announced the decision at KLSCAH's 103rd anniversary dinner tonight.
She said Anwar had told her to find a solution during the visit to the institution.
Hannah said the federal territories land committee subsequently approved the surrender and re-alienation of the land for institutional use on Sept 14, with a lease tenure of up to 99 years.

She said the formal approval letter dated Oct 1 confirmed the land premium at RM1,000 while the total amount payable under the official land notice is RM5,011, inclusive of the first year’s land rent and administrative charges, with the annual land rent fixed at RM3,151.
She said the place was recognised as a national heritage building in 2007 as KLSCAH had played an important part in Kuala Lumpur's history.
She hoped KLSCAH would now be able to channel more of its resources towards maintaining the hall, preserving its heritage and continuing its work for the community.
Hannah also highlighted ongoing efforts by DBKL to study the preservation of traditional Malay villages in Sungai Penchala, including Kampung Palimbayan and Kampung Bukit Lanjan.
f1c77c67cb628c6b: PETALING JAYA: Perdana Menteri Anwar Ibrahim mengucapkan tahniah kepada Barisan Nasional (BN) atas mandat diberikan rakyat Melaka dalam PRN hari ini.
Beliau berharap amanah itu digalas dengan penuh tanggungjawab demi kesejahteraan negeri dan rakyat.
“Penghargaan kepada seluruh pengundi yang menunaikan tanggungjawab demokrasi serta jentera dan semua calon Pakatan Harapan (PH) yang bekerja keras.
“Kini masanya untuk kita melangkah ke hadapan dengan mengutamakan kepentingan rakyat,” katanya di Facebook.
Anwar yang juga pengerusi PH berkata, kerajaan persekutuan akan terus memperkukuh kerjasama dengan kerajaan negeri Melaka demi memacu pembangunan serta menjamin kesejahteraan seluruh rakyat.
BN dan Perikatan Nasional (PN) yang membentuk kerjasama pada PRN Melaka berjaya meraih kemenangan di 24 daripada 28 kerusi DUN, sekali gus mendapat mandat menubuhkan kerajaan negeri.
PH pula hanya menang empat kerusi daripada 24 DUN ditandinginya.
56c7a5ba440fcb52: THE world must be watching developments in Indonesia with growing concern, particularly those living in this region. Indonesia is, after all, Southeast Asia's most populous country and largest economy, a G20 member and a founding member of Asean.
The world is already grappling with numerous challenges, and every country must deal with them as best it can.
Unfortunately, President Prabowo Subianto's government is also facing a series of domestic challenges emerging almost simultaneously.
The challenges are considerable.
The rupiah has weakened to a record low against the US dollar, falling beyond the levels reached during the Asian financial crisis of 1997-98.
Students have taken to the streets to protest against rising living costs, among other grievances.
Foreign investors have also been withdrawing funds from the Indonesia Stock Exchange at a record pace.

Amid these challenges, forest fires have continued to affect parts of Kalimantan and Sumatra, fuelling public discontent as residents contend with health problems and disrupted livelihoods caused by the haze.
A stronger-than-expected El Niño also worsened fire conditions this year.
Prabowo can hardly be blamed for these misfortunes emerging before he is even halfway through his presidential term.
He must now also contend with the inevitable political fallout.
Prabowo was elected on a wave of popular support after forging a political alliance with his predecessor, Joko Widodo, and choosing Joko's son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, as his running mate.
This week, Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka resigned amid controversy over whether his academic qualifications met the requirements for the post.
His resignation comes amid growing speculation about a widening rift between Prabowo and Joko, who left office after 10 years with considerable public goodwill.

This seems like an unfortunate replay of elite politics playing out in the Philippines where President Ferdinand Marcos Junior forged a ticket with Sara Duterte, the daughter of his predecessor, Rodrigo Duterte, and won by a landslide.
Vice-President Duterte is again facing impeachment proceedings.
If convicted by the Senate, she would be barred from holding public office, potentially derailing her presidential ambitions.
Could a similar political rupture occur between Prabowo and Joko's family?
Political tensions in Jakarta have yet to reach such a level.
Those of us who wish Indonesia well must hope that such a rupture can be avoided.
As we watch anxiously the happenings in Indonesia, we must hope for an orderly and measured political resolution.

Whatever conspiracy theorists may think and say, Indonesia's near neighbours have much more to gain from its rising prosperity and political stability than if it were to wade into another round of political and economic uncertainty.
The great diversity and physical sprawl of Indonesia make it a challenge to govern at the best of times. Nothing in neighbouring countries comes close by comparison.
The writer views developments in the nation, region and the wider world from his vantage point in Kuching

47b57161d51e2983: MELAKA: Unity, solidarity and sacrifices by grassroots machinery were among the factors behind the success of the Perikatan Nasional-Barisan Nasional cooperation in the 16th Melaka election.
Pas vice-president Datuk Idris Ahmad said these strengths had enabled the coalition partners to overcome their opponents' advantages.
"True strength lies not only in financial resources or media dominance, but also in unity, a shared understanding and collective action, which are reflected through the ballot box.
"With this strength, no matter what kind of tsunami comes our way, we can prevail. This has been proven in the Melaka election," he told reporters after the announcement of the election results.
He said the victory in Melaka should serve as a foundation for strengthening political cooperation at the national level ahead of the next general election.

"God willing, we will strengthen it further. It began to take root in Johor, then blossomed in Negri Sembilan, and today it has borne fruit. God willing, its shade will extend to Putrajaya next," he said.
Idris also thanked Melaka voters, particularly young people who had their first opportunity to vote under the Undi18 policy.
He said young voters had shown their potential to become agents of change and play an important role in shaping the country's political landscape.
"This time, it has been proven that young people are agents of change and a factor that can bring about political change at the national level.
"We hope this will bring continued benefits in the lead-up to the next general election," he said.
Earlier, Election Commission chairman Datuk Seri Ramlan Harun said BN secured a simple majority after winning 15 of the 28 state seats in the 16th Melaka election, as of 9.40pm.
He said the results allowed BN to form the state government with a simple majority.
b5ba97bd5ade6c4d: MELAKA: Kemenangan DAP di Ayer Keroh membuktikan parti itu masih mendapat sokongan meluas daripada pengundi pelbagai kaum, kata Pengerusi DAP Melaka Khoo Poay Tiong.
Beliau berkata kejayaan mempertahankan kerusi itu amat bermakna memandangkan ramai sebelum ini menjangkakan DAP akan tewas susulan kerjasama Barisan Nasional (BN) dan Perikatan Nasional (PN).
"Ayer Keroh kawasan campuran dengan komposisi pengundi pelbagai kaum yang agak seimbang," katanya pada sidang media di Ibu Pejabat DAP Melaka.
Menurutnya, kemenangan itu membuktikan calon DAP masih mendapat sokongan meluas daripada pengundi.
Sebelum ini, penganalisis politik yang juga bekas Ahli Parlimen DAP, Ong Kian Ming, menyenaraikan Ayer Keroh antara kerusi berisiko tewas kepada gabungan BN-PN.
Pengundi Cina membentuk 46% daripada keseluruhan pengundi Ayer Keroh, diikuti Melayu (44.1%) dan India (8.2%).

Calon DAP Kerk Chee Yee mempertahankan kerusi itu selepas memperoleh 14,078 undi dengan majoriti 5,604 undi, menewaskan Michael Gan (PN), Hamnaim Mohamad (Bersatu) dan Muhaimin Lau Abdullah (Bersama).
DAP turut berjaya mempertahankan tiga lagi kerusinya iaitu Kota Laksamana, Kesidang dan Bandar Hilir.
Khoo mengaitkan kejayaan itu dengan hubungan lama DAP bersama pengundi di Melaka, selepas parti berkenaan bertapak di negeri itu sejak 1969.
Bagaimanapun, beliau mengakui DAP sedih apabila rakan komponennya dalam Pakatan Harapan (PH) gagal memenangi sebarang kerusi.
Beliau mendakwa BN dan PN memainkan politik identiti berteraskan penyatuan Melayu dan Islam sepanjang kempen pilihan raya.
"Saya percaya strategi ini menyukarkan parti komponen kami dalam pilihan raya kali ini," katanya merujuk kepada Amanah dan PKR yang gagal memenangi sebarang kerusi.

8286f39acdd84538: PETALING JAYA: The Melaka election results have reflected the confidence of voters in the efforts of Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional to unite Malay-Muslims, PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang said tonight.

45e5e0b06cdb4b4f: MELAKA: The DAP victory in Ayer Keroh shows that the party continues to enjoy broad multiracial support from voters, Melaka DAP chairman Khoo Poay Tiong said tonight.
He said retaining the seat was particularly significant as many had expected a DAP defeat after Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional joined forces.

“Ayer Keroh is a mixed constituency, where the composition of voters from different communities is relatively balanced,” he said at a press conference at Melaka DAP headquarters. He said the victory showed that the party's candidate continued to receive broad support.
Political analyst Ong Kian Ming, a former DAP MP, had previously identified Ayer Keroh as one of the seats that Pakatan Harapan risked losing because of the BN-PN alliance.
Chinese voters make up 46% of Ayer Keroh's electorate, followed closely by Malays at 44.1% and Indians at 8.2%.
DAP's Kerk Chee Yee retained the seat with 14,078 votes for a majority of 5,604 votes, defeating PN’s Michael Gan, Bersatu’s Hamnaim Mohamad and Bersama’s Muhaimin Lau Abdullah.
DAP also retained its other three seats: Kota Laksamana, Kesidang and Bandar Hilir.

Khoo attributed DAP’s performance to its longstanding relationship with voters in Melaka, where the party has had a presence since 1969. However, he said that DAP was saddened that its PH partners had failed to win any seats.

afef36194f1d5843: WASHINGTON: US transportation secretary Sean Duffy sought to assure Americans Saturday it remains "safe to fly" after an hours-long ground stop, but warned of more flight cancellations as airlines grapple with thousands of stranded passengers.

More than 20,000 flights were impacted by Friday's rare nationwide flight stoppage, and the effects were rippling across the industry, with more than 3,800 US flights already cancelled Saturday and another 2,100 delayed, according to tracking website FlightAware.
"Operations are slowly returning to normal this morning. Planes are pushing back, taxiing, and taking off, and it is safe to fly," Duffy said on X.
"You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most."

Duffy, an appointee of US President Donald Trump, thanked air traffic controllers, pilots and flight crews for their dedication and hard work during the crisis and added that "our top priority right now is making sure travellers get home safely to their families as quickly as possible."

The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos, but it has also raised serious concerns about the country's ageing infrastructure and how it could be particularly susceptible to cyberattacks.
Homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday dismissed speculation about a coordinated cyber assault on the US or any link to the Microsoft outage that affected services worldwide.

But as US lawmakers and others on Saturday called for investigations into what caused the massive disruption and whether the country is adequately secure from cybercriminality, the government urged patience from travellers.
"We appreciate your continued patience as operations return to normal," the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement.
As of mid-morning Saturday, Trump, often quick to comment on social media on issues of such magnitude, has made no public statement about the ground stop.
e205fdbf6b8d4ee1: SINGAPORE-BASED tech group Megaspeed dealt in billions of dollars' worth of the world's most advanced AI chips, and its former director, Alice Huang, was this week outed as an alleged Chinese spy.
She was accused of having an affair with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang while digging up company secrets for Beijing.
Details about Alice Huang's life are vague, making it almost impossible to pin down where she lives, where she works, or when she was born.
But her influence undoubtedly spreads far and wide, from the nondescript Singapore office, to hulking data centres in Southeast Asia, to the gleaming boardrooms of Silicon Valley.
Her connection to cloud computing firm Megaspeed sits at the centre of the scandal.
Megaspeed touts itself as a company at the heart of the AI revolution, using Nvidia's advanced silicon chips to power high-performance computing inside vast data centres.
But it is also under investigation for serving a murkier purpose.
Megaspeed has allegedly helped Beijing skirt trade restrictions by sending Nvidia chips into China.
Beijing has denied allegations of spying, and Megaspeed said it was investigating if it had complied with export controls on the sensitive chips.
Singapore police opened an investigation in February 2025 into Megaspeed and other companies suspected of circumventing or violating export controls.

Alice Huang was interviewed as part of Singapore's probe. Although no charges were laid, she was barred from the city-state in February 2026 for providing inaccurate information to "down-play her role in Mega-speed".
A company linked to her acquired the Singapore arm of Chinese video game developer 7Road International in early 2023.
The 7Road name was then changed to Megaspeed International.
Huang was listed as a Megaspeed director for less than a year, taking the role between March and November 2023.
Her arrival coincided with a drastic change in fortunes, as Megaspeed pivoted from a little-known video game maker to one of Asia's biggest buyers of Nvidia chips.
Over two years, Megaspeed reportedly traded in upwards of US$4 billion worth of Nvidia chips.
Megaspeed has a Malaysian subsidiary that struck a deal in 2024 pledging assets to Apex Enterprise Solutions in Singapore as security in case of contractual breaches.
In June 2025, US investigators turned up at Megaspeed to carry out a "post-shipment verification", with Huang present, according to Singapore's Home Ministry.
That same day, Huang was interviewed by Singapore police, who impounded her passport.
By then, she and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had already been spotted together in public.
In one of their early outings together, they were seen mingling at an afterparty following the Computex trade show in Taiwan at the beginning of 2024.
The scandal has sparked national security fears.
China and the United States are fighting for supremacy in artificial intelligence, and Nvidia's market-leading products have become a major point of contention.
Nvidia controls an estimated 90 per cent of the market for the chips used to train and run AI models, and the US imposed rules in 2022 to restrict their sales to China.
In any case, the restrictions appear to have been circumvented.
A Chinese university tied to the nation's defence establishment was able to buy advanced Nvidia chips, according to procurement notices from October and September.
Alice Huang sits in the middle of a corporate web, connected to myriad shell companies, investment houses and major Chinese technology firms.
Corporate records filed in Hong Kong list her as a director of Nanjing Lingxing Technology, which operates the popular T3 ride hailing platform in China.
Other notable investors in Nanjing Lingxing Technology include Alibaba and Tencent, as well as state-backed carmakers like China FAW and Dongfeng Motor Group.
A corporate CV published by a Chinese investment firm details Huang's rapid ascent through the ranks of Asian investment banking.
She served in a senior role at HSBC around 2012, the resume claims, before moving on to stints at CITIC Securities and Shanghai Hexi Investment.

She was born in China's Hunan province, which she left to study media in Hong Kong, HK01 media reported. A CCTV reporter wrote on Weibo that she worked with Huang at the Chinese broadcaster, but later deleted the post.
The writers are from AFP

915f5496a895968f: The latest commercial crime figures released by Bukit Aman paint a worrying picture that should concern the police and the public.
Data for January to October this year show a 15.88 per cent increase in arrests and a 52 per cent rise in charges brought.
Despite the increases, losses from commercial crimes rose 30.95 per cent to RM5.25 billion from RM4.01 billion in the corresponding period last year.

More troubling is the 235 per cent surge in losses from e-financial crimes to RM280.72 million from RM83.71 million a year earlier. Police need to examine more closely why increased arrests and prosecutions have yet to translate into lower financial losses for Malaysians.
Have fraudsters and scam syndicates become more sophisticated, inflicting heavier losses on victims despite increased arrests?

If so, tackling commercial crime will require a more comprehensive approach involving intelligence-sharing, international cooperation and closer scrutiny of financial institutions, telecommunications companies and technology platforms.
Efforts to identify the masterminds behind criminal syndicates, trace stolen funds and disrupt the financial networks sustaining their operations must also be stepped up.
More resources must be channelled to intelligence and investigative work to dismantle these criminal networks.

The authorities must stay ahead of these criminals by monitoring financial transactions and tracing how ill-gotten gains move through local and international financial networks before being laundered.
Banks, money-transfer operators, telecommunications companies and foreign law enforcement agencies must work together to close loopholes exploited by operators of mule accounts.
In addition, a public awareness campaign is essential to educate people about the risks of commercial crime and how to avoid falling victim to scams.

Bukit Aman's Commercial Crime Investigation Department director Commissioner Datuk Rusdi Mohd Isa said the public must not trust calls, messages or offers of investment schemes from unknown individuals over the phone line or through emails.
People should never disclose banking details, passwords, one-time passwords (OTPs) or transaction authorisation codes (TACs) to anyone claiming to represent a bank or other trusted organisation.
While the police can pride themselves on the increases in arrests and prosecutions, the scale of financial losses shows that the battle against scammers and fraud syndicates is far from won.
White-collar crime is no longer confined to boardrooms. It has reached the homes of ordinary Malaysians, making the task of enforcement considerably more challenging.
