19d3409769297d89: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life.

Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely.

But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor.

Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble.

So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks so much. Great to be here.

I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.”

Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET?
It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019.

Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI.

Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff.

Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys.

The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.”

It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like?

It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do.

AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well.

I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world.

In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth.

What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years.
Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff?

Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment.

The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way.

In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close.

There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective.

I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.”

With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day.

I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning?

They put in some of that work in 2023. I think this year we’re seeing another big wave of interest and people making the time and making the headspace to get smarter on it. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for.

In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?”

We’re going to see. There’s a whole bunch of new people. I imagine you have a new cast of characters to go and brief about the technology and what it’s capable of. We’ll see if they have revitalized the institutions.
[Laughs] I’m sure it’ll be all fixed overnight.

They’re very excited today, but we’ll see how it goes. The other thing that I want to ask you about is the technology itself, the nature of the technology itself, and how you are thinking about it, and the nature of the companies that are making the technology.

The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. My favorite example of this is we have straight-up asked Anthropic if it thinks Claude is alive and the answer was not no. The answer was a long discursion into the nature of the word “alive.”
Well, it depends on what you mean by “alive” to start with.

It does. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood? It wasn’t us. Why are we talking about the requirement of flesh and blood to be alive?” And then some further conversation about the moral status of Claude is yet to be determined.
There’s a huge divergence here between the AI overviews most people experience in Google search and “the moral status of Claude is uncertain.” Where are you? How are you situated in that debate?

A big part of how I see our role at CSET as an organization, and then also my role as someone who is crossed between these worlds, is trying to translate and voyage to California and then bring back the artifacts and the recountings of my journey.

I definitely think that there are a lot of people who have used the free tier of ChatGPT, or they’ve used voice-based models, which generally do worse, or they’ve just used Google AI overviews and they’ve laughed at how stupid Google AI overviews are. They haven’t used agents and they don’t know what frontier models can do. So there is just a basic piece around what the current generation of models can do.

There’s a historical piece as well, which I find increasingly relevant as I’m now 10 years into working on AI and national security stuff. If you’re looking at this current moment in time, this snapshot, and saying, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” you have to situate that in the long history of people being like, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” for many, many values of X that have since become totally overcome by events.

You can go back and say, “Okay, well, here’s how we were talking about creativity, for example, five or 10 years ago.” Or we were talking about reasoning as this insurmountable thing before you had these new models come out. A huge thing that I am spending time on these days is not just the past and present of AI, but how companies are thinking about what they’re doing, especially the two leading companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, and this is true at Google, Meta, SpaceX to some extent as well.

This idea in the Bay Area that it’s just in the water, very normalized of, “Well, first we’re going to figure out how to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) and then we’re going to do that until we have superintelligence that is AI that vastly outstrips humans.” That’s taken for granted in a lot of circles at this point. I think there’s still a ton of alpha in just taking the fact that that is what they’re trying to do and just explaining what that means.

It takes a little while to lay out. “What is RSI? Why would you want to do that? What is superintelligence? What does that mean? Is that realistic?” All of that. But it is something I find myself spending a lot of time on these days, and something that there is increasing willingness to take seriously and to listen to in DC as well.

Lay that out for me. I think probably a lot of people listening to this show understand what you’re talking about, but we have a big audience. What do you mean by, “We’re going to do RSI and that will lead to superintelligence?”

The starting point here is these companies, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, were not set up to be consumer internet companies. A lot of people encountered this whole space after ChatGPT was launched. So the natural slot in their brain that they put a company like OpenAI or Anthropic into is a consumer tech company, where they have an app and I play with their app.

I cannot overstate how far that is from the vision of both companies when they started, and also the vision deep in the hearts of some of the top people at both of those companies. The vision deep in their hearts is we’re going to build machines that are as smart as or smarter than people. That is going to be amazing and it’s going to be a huge scientific achievement and it’s going to revolutionize the world and we’re going to be at the forefront of that and we’re going to do everything we possibly can to drive towards that.

That’s not a totally brand-new thing. We don’t have to do the whole history of AI, but it started as a field in roughly the 1950s with this idea of whether you can recreate human intelligence inside a machine. That’s kind of the starting point. If we’re talking about people like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, but also the core people inside, the researchers inside their labs, so your Alec Radfords or your John Schulmans or people like that, that is the vision that got them into this space that is motivating everything that they do.

That’s been true since the beginning, since OpenAI was founded in 2015 and Anthropic in 2021. These days, the point that they’re getting to is this idea of RSI, recursive self-improvement, which again, is a very old idea. In the 1960s, this guy called I. J. Good, who worked with Alan Turing, talks about the possibility that you could build an ultra-intelligent machine, meaning a machine that is more intelligent than any human, and then that could build an even more intelligent machine and that could build an even more intelligent machine, which would kick off what he calls an intelligence explosion, meaning that the level of intelligence of the systems is exploding.

For decades and decades and decades, this was this theoretical idea of, “Well, if the AI gets smart enough, maybe it can take over building the next generation of AI or directly improving itself.” I think 2025 and 2026, we’ve started to see AI companies saying, “Okay, yeah, this theoretical idea… we’re actually starting to be able to do a minimal version of it in practice.”

It’s not handing over all the AI development to the AI, and it’s certainly not saying to GPT-6, like, “Okay, GPT-6, improve yourself.” That’s not what they’re doing. But they are progressively using AI for more and more parts of their overall R&D pipeline, and they are increasingly saying that they’re seeing acceleration from that. They’re seeing their own R&D getting faster and faster.

A lot of people elsewhere doubt this, but a lot of people inside the companies really think it. When Demis Hassabis says “we’re in the foothills of the singularity,” this is the kind of thing he means: We might be seeing that initial part of the exponential curve where the AI systems are building the next generation of smarter and smarter systems such that the hockey stick then goes up.

At this point, it’s been a part of the culture and a part of the goals for so long that I think people in these companies can lose sight of how totally insane that sounds to many, many people. So I feel like there’s a lot of value in just trying to lay out, “Here’s what they are trying to do. They might not be able to do it, but they might be,” and presenting that to a range of different people.

How would you manage that? Demis Hassabis saying “foothills of the singularity” is an all-time quote. I’m not 100 percent sure the people at Google knew he was going to say that on stage to end the conference.
Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI, announced a new version of the model a few months ago, and he was like, “Here it is. It’s Astra. It’s AGI now. Have a good time.” And he ended the call.
Are you there? Are we at AGI? Is this already here and we just haven’t noticed?

I actually wrote something about this. I do not want to say we have AGI. I do want to say we’ve reached the point where I think using AGI as a milestone is just totally unhelpful. The way I put it is the concept of AGI is kind of a fuzzy cloud, which you could think of as different parts of the cloud or different things people mean by AGI.

There are people who’ve complained about the term AGI for a long time. Ten years ago it was pretty helpful to be able to say, “Look, the AI systems we have today in 2016, they can all only do one thing and they can recognize speech or they can play Go or whatever, but we’re trying to build this bigger thing that we’re going to call AGI, which is human-level and it’s going to be so general purpose. It’s going to be amazing.”

That was a useful term then because this fuzzy cloud of different things AGI might mean was so far away, so you could just point at the fuzzy cloud. But at this point, we’re inside that cloud, meaning we’ve passed some definitions of AGI. A very basic one, for instance, would be even when ChatGPT came out as an artificial general intelligence. ChatGPT was very clearly not a specialist model that was only good at one thing, like recognizing credit card fraud or translation or whatever. It could do many, many, many things.
876d9b9d6cca8eea: PETALING JAYA: PRN Melaka menyaksikan Pakatan Harapan (PH) sekali lagi mengalami kekalahan, yang keempat berturut-turut selepas pilihan raya negeri di Sabah, Johor dan Negeri Sembilan.
PH hanya meletakkan 24 calon daripada keseluruhan 28 kerusi DUN Melaka, selain menjalin kerjasama pilihan raya dengan bekas sekutunya, Bersatu, yang bertanding di tujuh kerusi.
Gabungan pimpinan Anwar Ibrahim itu memenangi empat kerusi, berkurangan satu berbanding lima kerusi yang diraih pada PRN 2021.
Bersatu pula gagal memenangi sebarang kerusi, termasuk empat kawasan yang ditandinginya tanpa berdepan calon PH dan tiga lagi kawasan yang menyaksikan calon kedua-dua pihak bertembung.
Dalam kalangan parti komponen PH, DAP menunjukkan prestasi paling baik, seperti yang turut berlaku pada PRN Johor dan Negeri Sembilan.
DAP mempertahankan empat kerusi dimenanginya lima tahun lalu, manakala Amanah kehilangan satu-satunya kerusi yang dimilikinya.
PKR pula sekali lagi gagal memenangi sebarang kerusi, sama seperti pada PRN 2021.

DAP berjaya mempertahankan dua kubu kuatnya yang mempunyai majoriti pengundi Cina, iaitu Bandar Hilir dan Kota Laksamana, dengan selesa, selain mengekalkan penguasaan di dua kerusi campuran, Kesidang dan Ayer Keroh.

Bagaimanapun, Amanah menerima tamparan hebat apabila Naib Presidennya, Adly Zahari, yang juga bekas ketua menteri Melaka, tewas kepada calon PAS Ridzuan Sarif di Bukit Katil selepas menyandang kerusi itu selama dua penggal.
Adly, yang menerajui kerajaan negeri dari 2018 hingga 2020, merupakan calon paling menonjol diketengahkan PH, selain menjadi pilihan gabungan itu untuk kembali menerajui pentadbiran Melaka.

Kekalahannya di Bukit Katil, sebuah kerusi campuran dengan pengundi Melayu merangkumi kira-kira 64%, mencerminkan kegagalan PH secara keseluruhan menyaingi penyatuan undi Melayu hasil kerjasama Barisan Nasional (BN) dan Perikatan Nasional (PN).
PKR juga sekali lagi mencatat prestasi mengecewakan walaupun bertanding paling banyak kerusi dalam kalangan parti PH, mengulangi nasib yang menimpanya pada PRN Negeri Sembilan, Johor dan Sabah.

Sementara itu, persefahaman pilihan raya antara PH dengan bekas sekutunya, Bersatu, dilihat tidak mempunyai hala tuju dan komitmen yang jelas, sekali gus gagal memberi kesan bermakna terhadap keputusan pilihan raya.

Antara faktor yang mungkin menyumbang kepada keadaan itu ialah tentangan dalam PKR sendiri terhadap kerjasama dengan Bersatu, parti yang terlibat dalam Langkah Sheraton sehingga menyebabkan kejatuhan kerajaan PH yang memerintah di peringkat persekutuan dari 2018 hingga 2020.

Keputusan PRN Melaka dijangka menguatkan lagi desakan supaya pilihan raya umum diadakan lebih awal. Namun, persoalannya ialah bagaimana PH mahu menangani naratif penyatuan Melayu yang dibawa BN dan PN.
Kemenangan besar BN pada PRN Melaka 2021 tidak membolehkannya memenangi satu pun daripada enam kerusi Parlimen di negeri itu pada PRU 2022.
Bagaimanapun, keadaan itu berkemungkinan berubah pada PRU akan datang susulan penyatuan undi Melayu menerusi kerjasama BN-PN.

b2247d7941cd4412: MELAKA: After securing a sweeping victory in the Melaka election, Barisan Nasional chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi has described Perikatan Nasional as its "new strategic partner".

The two parties, which campaigned on a platform of Malay unity, won 24 of the 28 seats in the state assembly after forming an electoral alliance in which they agreed not to contest against each other. BN claimed 21 seats while PN won three.
Zahid said he hoped the election victory would mark the beginning of greater unity among Malaysians, including those with differing political views.

“Let bygones be bygones. Let us unite regardless of our political backgrounds,” he said at a press conference here after the alliance declared victory. “May this blue wave continue to spread throughout the country,” he said.
Zahid expressed his appreciation of PN, which he described as BN’s “new strategic partner”.
BN is a member of the federal unity coalition with Pakatan Harapan and East Malaysian parties, while PAS, the lynchpin of PN, sits on the opposition bench.
PN was formed by PAS and Bersatu a year after an alliance of PAS and Umno, known as Muafakat Nasional, collapsed in 2019.

5a02911d38d3a648: MELAKA, Nov 14 — Barisan Nasional (BN) and Perikatan Nasional (PN) have stormed to an emphatic two-thirds supermajority in the Melaka state election, capturing a combined 24 of the 28 state assembly seats, according to unofficial results tonight.
In a sweeping victory that consolidated the ruling coalition's regional dominance, BN triumphed in 21 constituencies on its own, matching its 2021 seat benchmark, while PN captured three seats.
The joint tally of 24 seats represents one more than the two coalitions achieved when contesting separately five years ago, decimating Pakatan Harapan (PH) to just four urban enclaves.

BN chairman Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi thanked voters across the state for delivering a resounding mandate, while Amanah leader Adly Zahari conceded defeat on behalf of PH, stating that the coalition would focus on rebuilding its grassroots strength.

Incumbent Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh secured an unassailable mandate to remain at the helm of the state administration, retaining his Tanjung Bidara seat with an unofficial majority of 8,650 votes, an exponential increase from the razor-thin 364-vote margin he secured in 2021.
BN also registered runaway majorities across rural and semi-urban bastions, led by a 12,036-vote cushion in Sungai Udang, which it successfully wrested back from PN, and 11,742 votes in Serkam.
BN's closest battle unfolded in Machap Jaya, where it held off a determined charge from PH's Ginie Lim by 1,925 votes after trailing in early ballot boxes.
PH suffered major political casualties across the state, losing former chief minister Adly in his Bukit Katil backyard to PN's Ridzuan Sarif.
The federal ruling pact took another severe hit in Paya Rumput, where Azman Abidin, political secretary to Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, was ousted by PN.

PH was ultimately reduced to its four traditional urban Chinese-majority strongholds of Kesidang, Ayer Keroh, Kota Laksamana, and Bandar Hilir, each retained by DAP with comfortable margins surpassing 5,000 votes as MCA failed to reclaim lost ground.
PN's three victories were swept entirely by PAS-affiliated candidates, who retained Bemban while capturing Bukit Katil and Paya Rumput out of the five seats allocated to the coalition.

Conversely, Bersatu suffered a humiliating statewide wipeout after fielding candidates in seven seats under its own logo following an acrimonious split with PAS. The party was dismantled in Sungai Udang, where its candidate polled just 1,522 votes against the winner's 13,558, with its best showing in Pantai Kundor still leaving Dr Asmah Samat trailing BN's Tuminah Kadi by 2,177 votes.
Newcomer Parti Bersama Malaysia again failed to win any of the seats it contested, while independent contenders were similarly shut out.

f58a9f93def6063a: MANILA, Nov 14 — Nearly 90 per cent of the proposed Code of Conduct (COC) in the South China Sea has been agreed upon by Asean and China, with Malaysia optimistic that negotiations can be concluded soon.
Foreign Minister Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan said negotiations were in their final stage, although several outstanding issues still required political decisions.
He said certain sensitive terms and provisions also needed mutual agreement among the countries involved.
“Malaysia, as the country coordinator for Asean-China relations, is committed to ensuring that the negotiations are concluded as soon as possible.

“Nearly 90 per cent of the terms, paragraphs and wording in the document have been agreed upon. However, some words may be sensitive to certain countries but not to others,” he told Malaysian journalists after attending Asean foreign ministers’ meetings here today.
Mohamad said the three-year target previously set to conclude the COC negotiations would expire this year, with efforts now focused on aligning the positions of the littoral states involved.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that watched movies, made sacrifices, got crafty, and aged backwards.

First, scientists learn how primates make meaning out of visuals by peeking into the brains of monkeys as they watch Despicable Me. Then: human sacrifice as climate “crisis rituals,” the fingerprints of prehistoric children, and the longevity secrets of ants.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens, or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files.
Humans watching monkeys watching Minions
Raghavan, Vinay S et al. “During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.” JNeurosci.

Settling down to watch a film is often viewed as a way to relax and shut our brains off for a while. Our brains, however, beg to differ—they are as busy as ever when interpreting videos, according to a new study based on brainwaves of humans and primates as they watch movies and short clips.

To better understand how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes, researchers studied eye movements and electroencephalogram (EEG) readings of neural activity in dozens of humans, as well as two macaques, as they watched videos.

“Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high level meaning across these ‘snapshots’ remains a mystery,” said researchers led by Vinay Raghavan of the City College of New York. The new results hint that “visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process,” the team said.

Human participants with EEG electrodes attached to their scalps (the “scalp movie dataset”) watched a selection of films including The Big Sick, The Peanut Butter Falcon, Whiplash, Room, Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, The Tomorrow Man, Dom Hemingway, Life After Beth, Woodshock, and The Comedian.
“Participants were instructed to watch the movie as they would normally watch a movie,” the team said.

A different “intracranial dataset” included several human patients and two rhesus macaques, the latter of which had electrodes implanted inside their skulls. This group watched shorter videos, including 10-minute clips of Despicable Me in both English and Hungarian, a 4.3-minute clip of the short film The Present, and three 5-minute clips of documentaries featuring macaques.

Taken together, the datasets revealed that the brain responds to “semantic novelty”—meaning new semantic or conceptual information that crops up over the course of a video—which is measured through patterns of short-gaze “fixations.” The study also suggests that many brain regions beyond visual processing are involved in this ability to draw meaning from scenes.

“These results challenge traditional vision models that treat fixations as independent snapshots and highlight the importance of considering the temporal dynamics of eye movements and the predictive nature of visual processing,” the team concluded.

In addition to opening a new window into the mind, the study raises the irresistible yet unanswerable question of what macaques make of Minions. Alas, here we must confront the limitations of the knowable universe.
In other news…
Relatively peaceful—apart from the odd mass human sacrifice
Snyder, Thomas and Klaus, Haagen. “Pax Lambayeque? Trauma, interpersonal violence, and environment over 3,000 years in the Lambayeque Valley Complex, Peru.” Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology.

When climate-related disasters struck ancient Peru, some cultures responded with mass human sacrifices to appeal to the cosmos. For example, at least 107 adult men were sacrificed in six closely-timed events at Huaca de la Luna around 550–600 CE, and more than 140 children and 200 juvenile camelids were sacrificed at the Huanchaquito-las Llamas site around 1450 CE.

These ritualized killings often coincided with flooding and freak weather related to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, the natural climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean that cycles through a warm “El Niño” phase and a cooler “La Niña” phase. The Huaca de la Luna sacrifice, for instance, occurred during a so-called “mega-Niño.” This connection inspired researchers to determine if environmental conditions were also linked to interpersonal violence outside of these ceremonial “crisis rituals” that were organized by elites.

The team conducted a meta-analysis of the skeletal remains of 1,633 individuals that lived in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley over the course of 3,000 years before the arrival of Europeans. The remains presented “no strong evidence for an association between environmental factors and interpersonal violence” and suggested “that non-ritual violence in the Lambayeque Valley Complex was rare (1.6%),” according to the study.

The mass sacrifices reflect “the sometimes lethal relationships between human behavior, cultural norms, and the environment—and are frequently used as cautionary allegories regarding the ongoing climate crisis,” said authors Thomas Snyder of New York University and Haagen Klaus of George Mason University.
Time to add “prevention of ritualized human sacrifice” to the list of reasons to address climate change. Worth a shot?
Before Play-Doh, there was clay-doh
Davin, Laurent et al. “Modelling symbols among the first-sedentary communities: Emergence of clay figurines in Epipaleolithic Southwest Asia.” PLOS One.

The fingerprints of children who lived 15,000 years ago in the southern Levant are preserved on clay artifacts, a discovery that exposes “a rare direct testimony of inter-generational knowledge transmission in a hands-on apprenticeship,” according to a new study.

Archaeologists studied 154 clay figurines that were unearthed across three archaeological sites in Israel, including a subset depicting birds, a gazelle, and two human forms. Crafted by the Natufian culture, these artifacts represent “the earliest evidence of a figurative clay tradition in Southwest Asia where it marks an important step in the evolution of human technology,” said researchers led by Laurent Davin of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

Because these people sculpted the artifacts by hand, fingerprints are occasionally spotted on the clay, revealing the contributions of children and adults. In some cases, a preserved “succession of gestures on the wet clay suggests that, during the modeling sequence, an adult passed on the figurine to a pre-pubescent child,” the team said. “Therefore, these artefacts could be interpreted as portable figurative mnemotechnic devices related to children’s learning of traditional beliefs and ethno-ornithological knowledge.”

It’s so evocative to see the preserved touch of a child who lived so long ago, capturing a moment of skill-building and, perhaps, play. While we don’t know exactly what these figurines meant to their crafters, their survival is a testament to human creativity and imagination.
The ants are Benjamin-Buttoning
Cole, Blaine J. and Wiernasz, Diane C. “A replaceable soma enables negative senescence in harvester ants.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

We humans are used to a pretty standard life cycle: Birth, reproductive years, a decline in fertility, and an inevitable slide toward mortality. But a multi-decade study of ants reveals that some colonies operate as “superorganisms” that display increased reproduction and decreased mortality rate with age, reversing the course of normal senescence.

Researchers who gathered 34 years of data on 3,285 colonies of the western harvester ant (Pogonomyrmex occidentalis) discovered that these groups “display reverse aging,” according to their new study.

“We will show that colonies of P. occidentalis not only have extraordinary longevity, but that their pattern of aging differs dramatically from that of most insects,” said authors Blaine J. Cole and Diane C. Wiernasz of the University of Houston. “Colonies exhibit negative senescence—increased survival and reproduction with greater age.”

This finding does not mean that individual ants are aging in reverse; worker ants live and die normally in these colonies. However, the larger superorganism becomes an unusual “non-senescing form.” While the ants go marching one by one, the colony’s lifespan adds up to a larger sum.
Thanks for reading! See you next week.

037e089a5d550c90: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.

Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.

“Having digital systems is important, but what matters is whether the information can be cross-checked to ensure that the quantity and value declared in the documents match the actual goods being exported,” he said in a statement.

He said discrepancies between declared values or quantities and actual cargo shipments could affect government revenue, create unfair competition among businesses and undermine confidence in Malaysia’s commodity trade.

Maritime Network managing director Datuk Seri R. Jeyenderan said Malaysia already had various electronic systems and government agencies responsible for monitoring export declarations, permits and supporting documents.— Bernama pic

Jeyenderan said Malaysia should consider whether its existing systems could be better integrated so authorities can track export information from the time goods are declared and loaded onto vessels until the shipments reach their destinations.

He said this was particularly important for commodities such as palm oil and petroleum, where large volumes of cargo pass through ports and may involve several parties, including exporters, shipping companies, storage operators and buyers.
“Authorities should be able to establish whether the goods declared by an exporter are consistent with the actual cargo loaded onto the vessel and the documents accompanying the shipment,” he said.

He said better coordination between the Royal Malaysian Customs Department, port authorities, commodity regulators and shipping operators could help identify discrepancies earlier and reduce the risk of revenue leakage.

Meanwhile, maritime analyst and scholar Nazery Khalid said that while it was understandable for multiple agencies to be involved in the process, they should break down institutional silos and work more closely together.
He said this was important to ensure documentation, monitoring, inspections, testing and enforcement were carried out effectively and transparently.
Nazery said digital technology should also be used to help the agencies coordinate, so they can share data and improve visibility across supply chains.
“This would allow the agencies to make more informed, data-driven decisions and strengthen oversight of commodity exports.

“This would also strengthen confidence in Malaysia’s export and trading systems, prevent revenue leakages such as unpaid taxes and unaccounted foreign exchange outflows, and mitigate public health risks arising from the misdeclaration of commingled cargo, such as blended palm oil,” Nazery said.

77103068193881cc: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces.

The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news.
As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like. Or, for that matter, other US tech giants.

Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners.

The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks.
A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill.

Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud."
A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't."

The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly."

Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure. Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted.
Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty.

Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register: "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure.
"Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy."

Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®
43cc5e36cf4870f2: LUMUT, Nov 14 — The Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency (AKPS) continues to operate as usual nationwide, unaffected by the decision to return its director-general to his parent organisation, the Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM).

Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said as the officer was on secondment from the police force, further administrative matters would be handled by the relevant agency, pending the appointment of a successor.

“We have not reached that stage (of appointing an AKPS director-general) yet. Let’s settle things one at a time. However, I can assure you that AKPS operations will not be affected because the agency plays an important role, as its name suggests — the Malaysian Border Control and Protection Agency.

“We cannot allow the entire organisation to come to a standstill just because its director-general is involved in a transfer. That is not how it should be,” he told reporters after officiating the Madani Kita Programme (PMK) and the 2026 handover ceremony for the People’s Volunteer Corps’ (Rela) Kampung Angkat Madani (Madani Adopted Village) and Sekolah Angkat Madani (Madani Adopted School) initiatives at Kampung Sungai Tiram here today.
He was responding to a question on the current status of the AKPS director-general’s position and when it was expected to be filled.

He said Home Ministry secretary-general Datuk Dr Awang Alik Jeman had been directed to give special attention to the agency’s management, while any court proceedings would be allowed to take their course in accordance with the law.

Saifuddin Nasution added that field reports showed that AKPS personnel remained effective in carrying out their duties, having foiled several smuggling attempts, including the recent arrest of two individuals who attempted to bring a large sum of cash through a route to Singapore.
On October 29, the Home Ministry decided that AKPS director-general Datuk Seri Mohd Shuhaily Mohd Zain would return to duty with the PDRM.
Mohd Shuhaily was appointed AKPS director-general for a two-year term from July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2027.

Meanwhile, on today’s programme, Saifuddin Nasution said the government had allocated RM500,000 for improvement works at four locations under the Madani Adopted Village initiative, and RM100,000 for a school under the Madani Adopted School initiative, bringing the total allocation to RM600,000.

The four Madani Adopted Village locations comprise Masjid Al-Ismailiah, where a cooking hall, storage room and covered walkway will be built; Sekolah Rendah Agama Rakyat (SRAR) Al-Hidayah, where the building will be repaired and the fence replaced; Surau Haji Lot, where the open-sided hall, cooking hall and women’s prayer area will be upgraded; and Surau Parit Haji Dollah, where handrails, a PA system, new carpets and solar lights will be installed.

Meanwhile, Sekolah Kebangsaan (SK) Sungai Tiram received an allocation under Madani Adopted School for painting works, replacement of gutters and maintenance of its four-storey building, as well as the conservation of its heritage wooden school building, including termite treatment, to improve the comfort of the school community.

“We have 11 agencies, each implementing one programme, and this is now the third year of the initiative. This means we have reached at least 33 villages, with allocations ranging from RM500,000 to RM1 million. The good thing is that none of the projects we have undertaken has been abandoned,” he said.

The PMK, which brought together about 2,000 participants, also featured various community and spiritual activities, including congregational Subuh prayers, religious talks, Rela’s Ziarah Kasih visits to the homes of two underprivileged residents, as well as free services such as haircuts and motorcycle engine oil changes, alongside Rahmah and Agro Madani Sales. — Bernama

c19e10ec91ee1c7d: LUMUT, Nov 14 — The Home Ministry acts solely as the implementing agency for the Pardons Board’s decisions on a prisoner’s sentence, including house arrest.

Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said the ministry was not in a position to comment further on calls from various quarters regarding eligibility for house arrest, as pardon petitions fall outside its jurisdiction.
“So whether a pardon petition is discussed, considered and decided or not, that is not within the Home Ministry’s scope of responsibility.

“But if a decision is made, our job is to carry it out. Whether the sentence is reduced, set aside, or the person is released or placed under house arrest, our job is to implement it,” he told reporters.

He was speaking after launching the Madani Kita programme and the 2026 handover ceremony for the Malaysia Volunteers Department (RELA) Madani Adopted Village and Madani Adopted School at Kampung Sungai Tiram near here today.

Saifuddin Nasution was commenting on media reports about a recent statement by Parti Amanah Negara (Amanah) president Datuk Seri Mohamad Sabu that house arrest should not be a privilege reserved for certain groups, but should be considered fairly for all eligible prisoners.

On November 6, the Kuala Lumpur High Court allowed former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Tun Razak, 73, to serve the remainder of his prison sentence in the SRC International Sdn Bhd case under house arrest at his residence in Langgak Duta, effective immediately until August 23, 2028.

Expanding on the legal perspective, Saifuddin Nasution said the right to submit a pardon petition is always open to any individual, regardless of status or background, once all judicial processes in court have been completed.

He said petitions submitted by prisoners while serving their sentences would be raised for the Pardons Board’s consideration at the federal level or before the Ruler or Sultan in their respective states.
“If there is a view that everyone should be given equal treatment, from a legal standpoint, that right already exists.
“As I said earlier, the first part is that anyone can apply. Whether the petition is entertained or not is another matter,” he said. — Bernama

f580b57a22b39ed9: MELAKA, Nov 14 — [9.25pm] Barisan Nasional chairman Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi has thanked Melaka voters for the mandate given to his coalition and Perikatan Nasional (PN) in the state election, in a statement issued on behalf of both parties.

The thanks follow an unofficial claim of a sweeping win by the BN-PN side, with BN secretary-general Datuk Seri Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki saying the two have won 24 of the 28 state seats, a clear supermajority in the state assembly.

If the claim holds, BN and PN together have taken all but four seats, which would leave Pakatan Harapan (PH) with just four, consistent with the seat-by-seat figures reported earlier, which showed PH holding only its urban seats of Kesidang, Ayer Keroh, Kota Laksamana and Bandar Hilir.

PH has conceded the results. Amanah’s Adly Zahari, a former Melaka CM, who lost his Bukit Katil seat to PN, said the coalition accepts the results and will focus on strengthening its efforts going forward.
The result will be read as a setback for PH, after DAP left the state government in July and the coalition went into the election as a rival to BN.

BN and PN are expected to work together in Melaka, but how formal that cooperation will be has not yet been spelled out. The figures remain unofficial until the Election Commission confirms the final results.
[8.45pm] Barisan Nasional (BN) has won the Melaka state election, with unofficial results as of about 8.35pm showing it past the 15 seats needed to form the government on its own.

Of the 24 seats declared so far, BN has taken 19, Pakatan Harapan (PH) four and Perikatan Nasional (PN) one. Four seats were still outstanding at that point: Bukit Katil, Paya Rumput, Kelebang and Ayer Molek.

BN’s results are decisive. Its biggest majorities came in Serkam (11,742 votes), Sungai Udang (12,036) and Telok Mas (10,903). It also captured Sungai Udang from PN, which held the seat in 2021, and kept Machap Jaya by 1,925 votes against PH’s Ginie Lim, after PH had led there at 7.19pm. Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusoh retained Tanjung Bidara with an unofficial majority of 8,650 votes, compared with just 364 in 2021.

PH’s results were concentrated in urban seats. It held Kesidang, Ayer Keroh, Kota Laksamana and Bandar Hilir, all by margins of over 5,000 votes, so MCA did not take the DAP seats it had said it was targeting.

PH’s worst result so far is in Bukit Katil, where PN’s Ridzuan Sarif leads Amanah’s Adly Zahari, who won the seat in 2021, by 3,224 votes. PN has also held Bemban and is claiming Paya Rumput, where BN secretary-general Datuk Seri Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki’s has announced a PN win over PH’s Azman Abidin, the pime minister’s political secretary.

The new party Parti Bersama Malaysia, which contested 16 seats, has not won any of the 24 declared so far, and neither has Bersatu. Bersama’s candidates have been well behind in each seat where they stood, which suggests the new party has not yet become a major factor in the vote.
If Asyraf’s declarations for Ayer Molek, Kelebang and Paya Rumput hold, BN would finish on 21 seats, matching its 2021 result, with PH on four and PN on three.
[8.30pm] The Election Commission has announced unofficial BN wins in Serkam, Ayer Limau, Merlimau, Tanjung Bidara, Rim and Ayer Molek, and a PH win in Bandar Hilir.
BN secretary-general Datuk Seri Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki has also declared BN wins in Ayer Molek and Kelebang, and a PN win in Paya Rumput. Those are party announcements, not yet confirmed by the EC.
Major develoments include caretaker Chief Minister Ab Rauf Yusoh retaining Tanjung Bidara with an unofficial majority of 8,650 votes, up from just 364 in 2021.
BN has so far claimed 17 seats: the 12 in the earlier list plus Rembia, Kuala Linggi, Gadek, Ayer Molek and Kelebang. PN has Paya Rumput, and PH has Bandar Hilir.
BN’s seats already allow it to form the state government by simple majority.
[8.05pm] Barisan Nasional secretary-general Datuk Seri Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said BN-PN has won 15 seats, the simple majority needed to form the Melaka government.
BN itself has declared unofficial wins in 14 seats. The two coalitions are also on track for a supermajority.
[7.50pm] Barisan Nasional secretary-general Datuk Seri Asyraf Wajdi has announced unofficial BN wins in Taboh Naning, Sungai Udang, Lendu and Tanjung Bidara, which is Chief Minister Ab Rauf’s seat.
These are BN’s own claims and have not been confirmed by the Election Commission.

[7.30pm] With all 28 seats having partial counts, BN leads in 17, PH in 7, PN in 3 and Bersatu in 1. A minimum of 15 is needed for a majority. Bersama is not leading anywhere, putting it on track for another duck.

Close contests are forming in Machap Jaya, where PH has overtaken BN by 419 votes and Kuala Linggi (by 257), both seats where BN led in the earlier counts. PN leads PH in Paya Rumput by 172, and Bersatu’s Dr Asmah Samat leads BN’s Tuminah Kadi in Pantai Kundor by only 27.

Caretaker Chief Minister Datuk Seri Ab Rauf Yusof leads comfortably in Tanjung Bidara (2,510 votes to PH’s 335 from 2,845 counted). DAP-held Kota Laksamana and Bandar Hilir have PH well ahead of MCA, by 5,002 and 2,666 votes respectively.
[7.15pm] BN is ahead in 13 of the 20 seats reporting so far, PH leads in five and PN in two, and Bersama is not leading in any of them.

PH leads in DAP’s strongholds of Kota Laksamana (1,459 votes to BN’s 356) and Bandar Hilir (849 to 154), with no sign of the MCA gains it was aiming for. Both are early counts, so margins could change.

[6.00pm] Melaka voters cast their ballots today to elect a new state legislative assembly, in a high-stakes election that serves as a critical test of Barisan Nasional's (BN) traditional fortress and the increasingly strained federal partnership between it and Pakatan Harapan (PH).
A total of 675,166 eligible ordinary electors were registered to vote across 240 polling stations statewide, which operated from 8.00am to 6.00pm.

Turnout at 5pm had reached the 70 per cent target set by the Election Commission, which indicated that it expects initial ballot returns to arrive by around 9.30pm, with a comprehensive final tally anticipated before midnight.
The battle for the 28-seat state legislature drew a crowded field of 79 candidates. PH mounted the widest campaign by fielding 24 contenders, closely followed by BN with 23 candidates.
Newly formed outfit Parti Bersama Malaysia launched bids across 16 constituencies, while Bersatu and the Perikatan Nasional coalition contested seven and five seats respectively.

The Melaka showdown follows previous state polls in Johor and Negeri Sembilan where BN asserted its dominance, highlighting an awkward political reality where the two dominant coalitions clash as fierce rivals in state contests despite sharing power at the federal level in Putrajaya.
Political analysts view the election as a crucial bellwether for how the fragile BN-PH pact will hold up heading into the next general election.

The ballot box outcome will also provide the first tangible measure of public sentiment regarding the controversial transfer of former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak to house arrest. The court-sanctioned home detention order was executed just days before polling, dominating campaign rhetoric across the state and overshadowing localised municipal issues.

651774b405c45576: BERLIN: Solar energy’s contribution to Germany’s net electricity generation is fast approaching a record of more than 100 terawatt-hours in a single calendar year, reported the German Press Agency (dpa).

By Sept 27, solar output had already reached 90.2 terawatt-hours, surpassing the 90 terawatt-hours generated during the whole of 2025, according to the German Solar Association (BSW-Solar), based in Berlin.

An unusually high number of sunshine hours and the continued expansion of photovoltaic capacity contributed to the figures, the association said, citing a generation update released by the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE on Saturday.
By contrast, 20 years ago, solar power generated just 2.2 terawatt-hours over an entire year.
The approaching record marks a milestone in Germany’s energy transition, said Carsten Kornig, managing director of BSW-Solar.
“Photovoltaics has developed from a niche technology into a cornerstone of our electricity supply,” Kornig said.
“Society as a whole benefits from this: through cheaper electricity, fewer energy imports and significantly lower climate-related damage.”
An electricity output of 100 terawatt-hours represents an enormous amount of energy. One terawatt-hour is equivalent to one billion kilowatt-hours.
For comparison, Hamburg consumed 10.7 terawatt-hours of electricity last year.
Households in Germany typically consume between 2,000 and 4,000 kilowatt-hours a year.
According to Germany’s Federal Statistical Office, 59.1% of all electricity generated domestically in the first half of 2026 came from renewable sources
Photovoltaics accounted for 17.8% of total domestic electricity generation, making it the country’s third-largest electricity source, behind wind power, the leading source, and coal.

bb69ceac1942f38a: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 14 — Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim today sought to correct claims that Malaysia’s debts had increased under his management as finance minister.
He attributed the rise to debts inherited from previous governments, such as those linked to 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
Anwar said the federal government tries its best to fulfil the needs of all but has limited finances.

“Now, among big issues, they say Anwar manage the economy, the debt increases,” he said during a meet-up before over 200 female trainees at the National Service programme’s Camp 515 here, rejecting the claim.

Anwar said the government had steadily reduced its budget deficit since he became finance minister in 2022, cutting the gap between spending and revenue from about RM100 billion that year to around RM90 billion, RM80 billion and RM70 billion in the following years.
He noted that total debt still increased.
“It increased because have to pay old debts — 1MDB debt, Felda debt, I have to pay RM980 million per year; Tabung Haji debt, RM10 billion have to pay,” he said.
He added that the government sometimes also had to pay other debts, such as those for weapons procurement.

The federal government’s fiscal deficit has narrowed from 5.5 per cent of gross domestic product in 2022 to 3.7 per cent in 2025, and is projected to ease to 3.6 per cent this year and 3.3 per cent next year.

The gap between government expenditure and revenue fell from RM100.84 billion in 2022 to RM92.44 billion in 2023, RM80.9 billion in 2024 and RM76.6 billion in 2025, but is projected to rise to RM80.5 billion this year before easing to around RM79 billion next year.
Earlier at the same event, Anwar said some countries start out well or progress because of their unity, but later face problems such as corruption and arrogance.
He described negative attitudes towards corruption, such as those who think it would be “stupid” for those who become prime ministers not to use their position to garner riches.
He said such a culture would “jahanam” – meaning destroy – a country.

e3678f0f8b26b10f: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 14 — Malaysia is currently facing thousands of cyber attack attempts every month, thereby demanding a faster and more robust level of preparedness from security forces in confronting new-millennium defence threats.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said that the country’s security landscape is no longer focused solely on conventional military threats; instead, cyber attacks, system intrusions, and terrorist cell movements have become the most critical challenges today.

“We face thousands of attack attempts in a single month. Therefore, we must strengthen (our defence), and last week I met with the top leadership of the Malaysian Armed Forces (ATM) to discuss strengthening the cyber security unit within the Armed Forces,” he said.

He said this while answering a participant’s question during the “Temu Anwar” session with the National Young Heroes of the National Service Training Programme (PLKN 3.0) at the 515 Territorial Army Regiment Camp here, today.

To illustrate the seriousness of the threat, Anwar referred to a recent airport operational disruption incident in the United States (US), which stemmed from telecommunications system issues in that major superpower.

“Think about how the United States, with all its sophistication, could not identify the cause, but there was an attack on the telecommunication system that caused it to crash. We are still waiting for the final report,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Prime Minister emphasised that the pattern of national defence and asset procurement must rapidly adapt to the sophistication of modern technology, such as drone operations, without neglecting conventional defence aspects.

Recognising the urgent need to empower both dimensions of defence, Anwar, who is also the Minister of Finance, said that the government has elevated the Ministry of Defence’s allocation to the highest level in history, making it one of the largest recipient ministries alongside the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Health.
He said this substantial funding is crucial to replace various obsolete conventional assets of the security forces, including naval vessels, aircraft, and armoured vehicles.

“Because of obsolete aircraft and broken-down tanks, we are spending on all of that. However, regarding these procurements, the government also wants to ensure that past problems — such as the use of agents and high commissions that resulted in multi-million ringgit ship projects being abandoned — do not happen again,” he stressed. — Bernama

73c8fc4d09d4061f: BEIJING: China and the US discussed tariff cuts, agricultural trade and other issues at their first trade council meeting on Friday, China's commerce ministry said on Saturday, days ahead of an expected leaders' meeting in Shenzhen next week.

"The two sides held candid, in-depth and constructive exchanges on implementing the outcomes of previous China-US economic and trade talks, including tariffs, a reciprocal 'US$30 billion-for-US$30 billion' tariff-cut arrangement, agricultural trade and other issues of mutual concern," the ministry said.
It did not say whether any agreements were reached. Both sides will continue using the council to address trade concerns, expand cooperation and reduce outstanding issues, the ministry added.

Following a September summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in Washington, the two sides proposed a US$60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts, including roughly US$17 billion worth of US farm goods that China imported in 2024, but the plan has yet to be finalised.

Chinese purchases of US farm goods other than soybeans are on track to hit a seven-year low this year, despite an agreement to buy US$17 billion annually through 2028, a Reuters analysis of customs data showed earlier this month, underscoring persistent uncertainty over the deal.
Beijing has repeatedly urged Washington to implement the US$60 billion tariff-reduction deal, calling it a prerequisite for increasing purchases of US farm goods.
The White House said Trump will meet Xi on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen.

8d46de7a63ed3c3a: SEREMBAN, Nov 14 — Negeri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim has confirmed the withdrawal of the contents of a letter submitted to the Malay Rulers dated September 17 as well as the position previously taken by members of the Negeri Sembilan State Executive Council (MMK) and effectively maintains the status quo regarding the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.
He said the letter, which has circulated widely, was sent to the Keeper of the Rulers’ Seal, Tan Sri Syed Danial Syed Ahmad, is self-explanatory.

“You have all read it, it has gone viral. The media has already commented extensively on it. So, I am confirming the letter. The letter is self-explanatory,” he told reporters after attending the Negeri Sembilan-level Deepavali Open House at the Seremban City Council (MBS) Hall here today.
Also present were the Undang of Luak Rembau, Datuk Sedia Raja Datuk Hassan Ab Hamid, and the Undang of Luak Jelebu, Datuk Mendika Menteri Akhirulzaman Datuk Azrin Khairi.
Following this confirmation, Ismail expressed confidence that the impasse which has persisted in the state for the past few months is nearing settlement.

Earlier, a letter dated November 10 had circulated, concerning the withdrawal of the contents of a submission made to the Conference of Malay Rulers on September 17, as well as the position previously held by the members of the State Executive Council (MMK).
The letter states that Ismail, together with 10 members of the State Executive Council (Exco), has unanimously decided to retract the contents of a letter dated September 17.

This decision takes into account a media statement by the Malay Rulers dated October 14, as well as an order from the Seremban High Court dated June 5, which maintains the status quo regarding the position of the Yang Di-Pertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.

The letter further explains that this decision was made to uphold the supremacy of the 1959 Negeri Sembilan State Constitution, preserve the order of the monarchical system, and ensure that the state administration continues to function in a peaceful and orderly manner.
“We reaffirm our commitment to always uphold our customs (adat) and to respect the position and authority of the royal institution within the state’s governance system.

“We also acknowledge the call by the Malay Rulers for any differences to be resolved through legitimate, authoritative, and credible channels, in a manner that is civil and consistent with our customs,” the letter reads.

The parties involved also expressed the view that efforts toward a resolution must be carried out with a strong sense of responsibility, in order to maintain harmony and stability in Negeri Sembilan and to prioritise the well-being of the people.
Meanwhile, Ismail could not provide further comment regarding the status of the 10 former Exco members, as he has not yet had the opportunity to have an audience with Tuanku Muhriz.

“As of now, since I have not yet had an audience with Tuanku, there is no further news. There have been no discussions regarding the status of the Exco members thus far. Once I have an audience [with His Highness], I will accept his views... for now, I cannot offer any comments,” he said.

The list of the 10 former Executive Council (Exco) members includes Datuk Mohd Faizal Ramli, Datuk Zaifulbahri Idris, Mustapha Nagoor, Siow Kong Choon, Siti Nur Umaira Hasim, Datuk Mohd Asna Amin, Datuk Mohd Razi Mohd Ali, Suhaimizan Bizar, Datuk Mohd Fairuz Mohd Isa, and Datuk Razali Abu Samah.
In another development, regarding the 2027 state budget, Ismail stated that he is still awaiting the consent of Tuanku Muhriz concerning the date for the legislative session.
“There is one point I must clarify to you all regarding the budget for the upcoming State Legislative Assembly session: the date I provided (November 26) is the date proposed by the state government.
“If His Highness consents to that date, we will proceed, it is entirely subject to his consent. The budget must be finalised before the end of the year,” he said. — Bernama
cb67596ce46fe189: MANILA: Canadian prime minister Mark Carney said Saturday that Ottawa had successfully concluded negotiations for a sweeping free-trade pact with the Philippines, as it seeks ways to reduce its reliance on the US.
The US-Canada trade war has ruptured what was once one of the world's closest economic partnerships.
While Canada's trade surplus edged up in September, driven by higher oil exports, US President Donald Trump's tariffs also pinched multiple sectors, data showed.
The deal with the Philippines was about six months away from being signed, Carney told reporters on the sidelines of a regional summit in Manila, where Trump is expected to arrive Tuesday.
He added a broader agreement was also in the works with the entirety of the 11-member Asean, with those talks "substantially concluded".
The pacts were "part of a strategy of developing a dense web of reliable partners to create more opportunities ... and reducing our relative reliance on the US," Carney said.
Calling the deal with Manila the "most comprehensive ... accord that the Philippines has signed," Carney said he expected trade between the countries to triple in the next decade.
Total trade between the two countries stood at about US$2.4 billion in 2025.
The deal will drop over 90% of tariff lines and cover areas ranging from agriculture to aerospace to artificial intelligence, Carney said without revealing specifics.

The deal with Asean, meanwhile, would be the "first trade agreement ... outside of Asia" for the bloc, Carney said, noting "more than US$50 billion a year in two-way trade, up nearly 25% in the past year".
In a separate statement, Manila said it expected the trade pact to be completed in the coming year.
Carney has maintained that trade with the US, a cornerstone of the Canadian economy, will not return to a pre-Trump normal and that his country must urgently diversify its trading relationships.

The Canadian prime minister is on a multi-nation trip that will next take him to the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh for a biennial Francophonie summit before he heads north for the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meetings in China's Shenzhen.
There, he will meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss Canada's trade commitments with Beijing, he said.
f178e7be327a714f: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say.

A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters.

Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms.

"Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said.

"I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable.
"So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently."
McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not.

"If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added.
"And we know your algorithm would."
Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too.
Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal.
She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly.
There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs.

"So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content."
Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories.
With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process.
Success of user reports trails away

As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially.

Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent.
Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures.

The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly.

Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests.

Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report, it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny.
Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment.

The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force.

England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves.

Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms.

She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.'

"In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered.
"So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®
