Melaka’s new political understanding offers a revealing experiment: can parties cooperate without asking citizens to surrender the right to question them?

The BN–PAS arrangement, described as tafahum siyasi, is significant not because former rivals can share a platform, but because it tests whether political reconciliation can accommodate disagreement, scrutiny and plural representation.

On Oct 21, Barisan Nasional chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi announced an understanding under which BN would contest 21 of Melaka’s 28 constituencies, with seven allocated to PAS and its partners. By nomination day, however, the reported arrangement had changed: BN was contesting 23 seats and Perikatan Nasional five.
That revision matters. Negotiated formulas reflect political intentions; the actual ballot determines the choices voters face.

Melaka BN chief Ab Rauf Yusoh subsequently described PAS as a strategic partner and said the parties would coordinate their campaigns and share a manifesto. PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang has indicated that cooperation could extend beyond Melaka.
These statements point to an evolving political relationship, not a binding prediction about future governments or voter behaviour.

The more interesting issue is the meaning of understanding itself. "Tafahum" suggests a willingness to acknowledge differences while finding common ground. In a diverse federation, that can be constructive.
Consent of the governed
Yet political accommodation becomes fragile when leaders mistake agreement among elites for consent among citizens.
Malay political cooperation and Malaysia’s multiracial constitutional character need not conflict, but their compatibility must be demonstrated through policies and conduct.

Consider representation. BN includes component parties whose constituencies and organisational histories differ from those of PAS. A shared campaign must explain how minority interests, religious freedom, education and local economic concerns will be addressed, without assuming that a joint platform erases substantive disagreements.
Equally, voters sympathetic to PAS deserve clarity about which proposals remain party positions and which commitments have been accepted by all partners.

A joint manifesto creates an opportunity to answer those questions. It should identify priorities that can be implemented within state powers, distinguish them from federal responsibilities and specify how competing proposals would be reconciled.
Without such clarity, a manifesto risks becoming a catalogue of agreeable aspirations, with contradictions emerging only after polling.
State and federal ties

There is also a federal dimension. BN participates in the national unity government alongside Pakatan Harapan, while its cooperation in Melaka involves parties associated with the parliamentary opposition.
Such asymmetry is neither inherently unlawful nor unprecedented in coalition politics. Nevertheless, it complicates public understanding of accountability.

Leaders should explain whether state-level cooperation changes their federal commitments and where the boundaries between electoral partnerships and governmental responsibilities lie. This question cannot be answered through rhetoric about loyalty alone.

State administrations make decisions affecting land use, investment approvals, local infrastructure and public services. Business confidence depends less on displays of unity than on whether policies remain clear and decisions can be challenged through established institutions.
Keeping spotlight on
There is no available evidence to establish that this electoral understanding has already changed investment outcomes; that would require separate analysis.

For Pakatan Harapan and other competitors, the appropriate response is substantive scrutiny rather than assuming that cooperation proves ideological inconsistency. Parties routinely negotiate across previous divisions.

What matters democratically is whether voters receive accurate explanations of those negotiations and meaningful policy alternatives. Criticism should focus on documented commitments, not speculative claims about hidden intentions.

The outcome of the Nov 14 election will reveal the choices made by voters, but not necessarily why each choice was made. Turnout, candidates, local grievances and broader party loyalties all interact. Claims that a new Malay consensus has emerged require evidence beyond leadership appearances and seat allocations.
Three questions
Electoral results should be interpreted cautiously, especially when several political relationships are changing simultaneously.

My assessment is that Melaka’s experiment should be measured against three questions: Are shared commitments sufficiently precise to be evaluated? Can participating parties disagree openly without paralysing the administration? And will citizens outside the parties’ principal constituencies enjoy equal access to representation and public services?
That obligation extends to opposition scrutiny, legislative debate and the independence of public institutions.
Political understanding acquires democratic meaning when it protects disagreement as well as cooperation.
Beyond Melaka, BN and PAS face a continuing choice between treating tafahum siyasi as a temporary arrangement among leaders and developing transparent principles that voters can examine.
Malaysia’s political maturity depends not on eliminating differences, but on making cooperation accountable to everyone affected by it.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.

60f80913d48f881c: One could be forgiven for thinking the world is hurtling towards an apocalyptic end and that humanity is about to reenact Mad Max, complete with spiked leather jackets and tribal warfare over the last remaining can of baked beans.

This is because more than 30 countries have recently issued “be prepared” warnings, sending preppers – those who prepare for the day when the grid goes down, the shelves go empty, and the world as we know it ends – into another frenzy of stockpiling and repetitions of “I knew it was coming”.

The world has become more dangerous—or at least appears so. With never-ending global conflicts, meteorological tantrums, and the instant, vibrating hum of social media algorithms pinging our dopamine receptors twenty-four hours a day, crises are no longer experienced; they are simulated in our heads before they even happen.

And social media amplifies crises in ways the older generation —who blissfully survived on slow-moving broadsheets and evening radio—never experienced. What once trickled down as boring administrative updates now floods our phones in real-time, inducing a collective, low-grade heart flutter.

When roughly 30 nations update their civil resilience playbooks in the same calendar window, algorithms do what they do best: they hallucinate a conspiracy. Social media sharing stitches these independent notices together into a terrifying mosaic of a coordinated global doom narrative.
Some viral headlines scream that something’s going terribly wrong; others claim governments are secretly preparing us for war and not telling us the whole story.
The world has always had its dangers; the difference today is that mechanisms for broadcasting anxiety have become infinitely more efficient.
The reality, as is so often the case, is wonderfully, boringly mundane.
To understand the October 2026 wave, we must separate routine government weather chores from modern media panic.

Take Malaysia. In late October 2026, the National Disaster Management Agency (Nadma) issued its thoroughly familiar seasonal reminder: citizens should “stock up sensibly” ahead of the northeast monsoon. The call was a practical, sober reminder to prepare for seasonal flooding—a ritual practiced faithfully every year since the 1990s across Southeast Asia.

Yet, this routine tropical memo collided on the calendar with a broader occidental wave, most notably the UK’s newly minted “Be Ready” campaign, launched under Prime Minister Andy Burnham to encourage multi-year resilience against generic short-term infrastructure glitches or cyberattacks.

When a seasonal flood warning in Kuala Lumpur and an all-hazards resilience campaign in London drop in the same fortnight, and more than 30 nations issue similar advisories, digital platforms turn it into a blockbuster movie trailer.
This happened despite every official source emphasizing the same thing: the advice was voluntary, gradual, and completely unrelated to any looming apocalypse.
So why are governments suddenly nagging us about emergency kits? Is the world ending? No. But our infrastructure has quietly evolved.

In the old days, if a local transformer blew out,your neighbourhood went dark, and we used a candle until power was restored. Today, because our banking, logistics, communications, and heating rely on digital infrastructure and interconnected power grids, a minor disruption cascades instantly across sectors.
Governments aren't warning us because war is at the door; they are doing it because hyper-connected societies are inherently fragile to short-term hiccups.

Predictably, human nature did what it always does. In the UK, Malaysia and elsewhere, some took to social media to urge people to stock up on food or actually cleared supermarket shelves of certain items, proving once again that panic is far more infectious than any virus.

They chose to ignore the advice to buy gradually and not panic. So much so that Nadma director-general Meor Ismail Meor Akim felt it necessary to issue a statement saying: “We should avoid such panic-buying messages. Sometimes, panic buying creates another problem, not a northeast monsoon disaster, but a shortage of goods instead. Just buy according to your needs.”
This brings us to the most important distinction of all: the gap between selfish hoarding and civic self-reliance.
When a government tells us to store a 72-hour buffer of water, a torch, and non-perishables, it isn't inviting us to join a doomsday cult. It is an exercise in decentralised pragmatism.

If households are self-sufficient for three days during a sudden power outage or flash flood, it keeps arterial roads uncluttered and emergency phone lines open for people facing actual life-and-death medical emergencies. And for other such emergencies.

An emergency kit isn't a survivalist fetish; it’s an act of civic hygiene. It’s the modern equivalent of bringing your own bucket to a neighbourhood fire instead of standing in the street screaming that the town is cursed.

Ultimately, these advisories don't signal a descent into martial law or long-term catastrophes. They reflect the tedious, necessary business of living in a complex world. Just as learning fire safety or getting vaccinated became the unremarked background noise of twentieth-century life, digital-age resilience is simply the new baseline of modern citizenship.
How should we respond?
We would do well to ignore the merchants of panic—whether they write viral social media threads or sensationalist headlines—and consult sober official sources instead.

By preparing quietly, rationally, and without melodrama, we insulate ourselves against minor tempests while preserving the sanity of the commonwealth at large. After all, if the world truly is coming to an end, panicking in the supermarket checkout queue is a singularly undignified way to greet the final curtain.

e0f47e1eef07df75: I drove to Seremban from my humble abode recently and covered 106km, if one rather disreputable GPS app is to be believed. My journey began on the northern route of the North-South Expressway which is numbered E1 as well as AH2 (for Asian Highway 2). If you've ever wondered what those small signs meant, you’re welcome!

At Sungai Buloh, the E1 morphed into the New Klang Valley Expressway (NKVE) and a new Asian Highway designation, the AH141. Later, I was back on some federal and city roads for a while before I rejoined the NSE at Sungai Besi on its southern route, numbered E2. Later at Bangi the E2 became the AH2 again.

On my return journey, the said disreputable GPS app took me through some quaint Seremban back roads where life appeared slower and I was reminded of the Penang I knew from many decades ago. I was then guided out of town and on to another expressway, the E21 or Lekas, yet another fancy acronym in this never-ending battle amongst toll highway concessionaires to pick the coolest name possible for their particular concession.

Lekas – fast in Malay – quickly took me away from Seremban’s charming old town and countryside and handed me over to the E18, the Kajang Dispersal Link Expressway or SILK, which is somehow a Malay acronym because apparently KDLE doesn’t sound very exciting. SILK smoothly took me onto the E27, the East Klang Valley Expressway, or EKVE, which probably means something cool in some language I’m not au fait with, perhaps French.

The E27 took me to the E19, the Sungai Besi Ulu Kelang Elevated Expressway (SUKE), which deposited me on the E33, the Duta Ulu Klang Expressway (DUKE), which also happens to be part of the AH141. I went from SUKE to DUKE, or from happiness to sadness, if your Malay is au courant.

Sad indeed, as there I was in a small sedan and not my usual thirsty but spacious old 4x4, which consumes a litre of petrol just coughing itself to a start. My back and knees and ego hurt while I looked up to other motorists rather than down on them – a rather unnerving and humbling experience indeed.

I duked my way out of the late afternoon traffic on the E33 back to the recently-traversed E1 incorporating the NKVE, and made my way home, which remains a humble abode regardless of how many French words I throw out to the hoi polloi in telling this story.
At this point, you’re probably close to screaming “Is there a point to all this?” Yes, there indeed are some points I’m trying to make, so hold on to your pantalons, dear readers.

I’ve driven on almost all major roads and highways and byways in Malaysia, especially on the peninsular side. But it appears Malaysia’s appetite for building toll expressways far exceeds my capacity to drive on each and every one of them.

I should have paid more attention when rich people objected to yet another expressway running through their neighbourhood and bringing down property values. Or when the conservation-minded people shouted about yet another toll highway cutting through some pristine nature preserve. All these mean yet another highway with a cute name and many toll booths is being born.

I’ve seen expressways that seem to just hang in the sky, and had I chosen the E12 Akleh elevated highway instead of the E33, or better still, taken the E12 and then still went on to the E33, my story would’ve been more fantastique and my knees more swollen.

Had fate and my GPS app taken me on slightly different routes, I could very easily have added the E6 Elite, the E20 Maju and maybe even the E38 SMART Tunnel to the list of highway concessions I helped enrich. With a few more diversions I could’ve also added the E31 DASH, the E23 SPRINT, the E6 Kesas, possibly the E11 LDP and the E13 LKSA, and closer to home, the E25 Latar and perhaps even the E35 GCE.

These are not all. Elsewhere and not quite taking me to Seremban are the E7 CKE, the E8 ECE, the E9 Besraya, the E10 NPE, the E26 SKVE, the E29 SPDH, the E30 NNKSB and the E37 LKS. These are all within the Kuala Lumpur-Seremban metropolitan area, and many of you probably drive on them regularly without realising how magnificent, intricate and widespread our toll highway network is.
But a blessing can also be a curse. More on that when the journey continues.

November’s patch release from Redmond tackles 1,093 vulnerabilities, fixing 63 “critical” flaws that can be exploited to seize control over a Windows system with little or no help from users. Nearly half of those critical bugs are remote code execution vulnerabilities. Overall, 535 of the flaws addressed this month allow an attacker to elevate their privileges on a vulnerable device.

This latest round of updates means Microsoft has shipped more than 5,100 security patches so far this year, a staggering number considering that a year ago Microsoft was averaging around 100 patches per month. Microsoft credits advances in artificial intelligence for helping to find (and fix) such a large volume of security bugs in recent months. Last month, Microsoft pushed more than 1,400 fixes.

According to Redmond, just one of the flaws is already seeing active exploitation: CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing bug in Outlook. The advisory for CVE-2026-124194 says it affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and editions of Microsoft Office.

Several other major software makers pushed security updates this week to fix critical weaknesses in their products. Apple on Monday released out-of-cycle security updates to fix at least nine vulnerabilities in iOS/iPadOS, macOS, watchOS and visionOS. Among the weaknesses reportedly fixed in Apple’s release include an iMessage flaw that could let a remote attacker join a group chat and receive its messages; the updates also fix a separate iMessage flaw that could let someone added to a group access messages sent before they joined.
Lee Neely, an instructor at the SANS Institute, noted that Apple backported the fix to iOS 18.

“I take notice when Apple releases fixes to more than two versions,” Neely wrote in a SANS newsletter today. “You really need to get to version 27.2.1 of their OSes and push folks who are holding onto devices which cannot run the current version. The best plan often involves setting an upgrade date for old hardware. Run through all your Apple devices and make sure everything is up to date, don’t assume the fixes went out automatically.”

Google this week released Chrome version 157.0.8103.50, which resolves nine security holes, including CVE-2026-125350, the sixth zero-day vulnerability this year for Chrome (this bug also is being patched in Chromium-based browsers like Edge). The latest Chrome version follows its November 3 release, which fixed 213 vulnerabilities. A new version of Mozilla Firefox out today (Firefox 160) resolves almost 100 CVEs, about half of them high severity.

Adobe today released patches for at least 110 vulnerabilities across a range of products, with nearly half of the flaws rated high severity. Adobe said there is no evidence any of the security holes it addressed this month are being actively exploited.

Chris Goettl, vice president of product management at Ivanti, said it’s easy for security teams at large enterprises to feel overwhelmed by the volume and criticality of patches from Microsoft lately. But he notes that while some 95,000 vulnerabilities have been assigned CVEs this year across all vendors, only 217 have so far this year been added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

“Roughly four in ten of this year’s exploited vulnerabilities sit in operating systems, endpoint software, browsers, and server platforms, which a continuous patch strategy can close quickly,” Goettl said.”The rest calls for exposure management alongside patching, especially the 44% that sit in edge devices and IT management or remote access tools, the internet-facing systems that hold privileged access. Teams that can quickly identify those assets, confirm exposure and act on confirmed exploitation can focus on the small slice of vulnerabilities attackers are actively using, while the rest stays on the normal patch cadence.”

Please don’t neglect to back up any important data if you haven’t recently; generally speaking, this is a task best accomplished before applying operating system updates. 2dcde4b665668871: Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called "big math" is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means, and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World, by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend.

Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London's Millennium Bridge.

An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019).

0f696e8c856711df: Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark.

DeepMind's physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There's the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. Essentially, it takes your instructions and uses live video to plan how the robot can accomplish the task. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that's Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5.

DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate.
4ac67656f256b571: From Jamaluddin Aziz

The announcement that the Islamic development department (Jakim) and central committee for applications for filming and performances by foreign artistes (Puspal) are investigating alleged elements of ritualistic worship at The Weeknd’s recent concerts at the Bukit Jalil national stadium highlights a recurring cultural tension in Malaysia.
As a critical media scholar, I view this controversy not merely as a clash over entertainment guidelines, but as a textbook case of “context collapse”.

Coined by media researcher Danah Boyd and further theorised with Alice Marwick in their seminal 2011 study in New Media & Society (“I tweet honestly, I tweet passionately: Twitter users, context collapse, and the imagined audience”), context collapse occurs when digital platforms flatten multiple, distinct audiences into a single space.

When content created for one specific cultural or artistic environment is stripped of its original framing and judged within an entirely different moral or ideological context, modern pop theatrics are easily misread as literal religious devotion.

To understand how context shapes interpretation, one need only compare The Weeknd’s Nov 4 and 5 shows with another massive event held at the exact same stadium just three weeks earlier: Konsert Tradisional Gema Bumantara by Biduanita Negara Siti Nurhaliza.
Both concerts drew tens of thousands of devoted fans who sang every lyric in unison and cheered wildly for their favourite performer.
Yet, the public and institutional reactions to these two sold-out spectacles could not have been more different.

In modern pop culture, intense audience enthusiasm is often loosely referred to as “fan worship”. Historically, words like “fan” (from the Latin fanaticus, meaning temple frenzy) and “icon” (from the Greek eikōn, meaning sacred image) do share etymological roots in ancient religious practice.
Today, however, these terms describe secular cultural admiration. When fans cheer at a stadium, they are participating in collective musical enjoyment, not a spiritual ritual.

Viewing both Bukit Jalil concerts through a critical media lens reveals three key dynamics driving these divergent reactions. First is the mechanics of context collapse. Critics of The Weeknd’s concert pointed to short social media clips showing a towering golden female robot sculpture and dancers in red hooded robes as evidence of pagan or machine-worship rituals.

As Marwick and Boyd’s framework demonstrates, when these visuals are detached from the full two-hour concert narrative and circulated online to audiences unfamiliar with Western pop-art tropes, context collapses.
Stripped of their theatrical framing, a futuristic sculpture by Japanese artist Hajime Sorayama meant to critique the hollowness of fame and materialism is flattened into a literal religious idol.

Second is embedded cultural context. In contrast, Siti’s concert operated within a shared, deeply understood local framework. Utilising classical floral visuals and orchestral staging without human statues, her performance aligned seamlessly with Malaysian cultural and religious norms.

Because audiences and regulators immediately understood the context of Irama Malaysia heritage, the collective euphoria in the stadium was celebrated as patriotic pride rather than scrutinised as spiritual misdirection.

At most, conservative critiques of such local shows rarely go beyond general moral cautions against lagha (worldly distraction or frivolous amusement), a far cry from the theological panic of syirik (idolatry) projected onto The Weeknd’s unfamiliar pop symbolism.
Third is audience literacy and intent. Context collapse assumes that audiences are passive consumers who absorb imagery literally.
In reality, modern concertgoers possess high media literacy. Tens of thousands of Malaysians attended The Weeknd’s show to experience Grammy-winning music and dystopian sci-fi stagecraft.

Treating theatrical props as acts of syirik (idolatry) ignores the crucial distinction between artistic metaphor and religious intent (niat), unfairly questioning the faith and intelligence of ordinary Malaysian fans.
Puspal plays an essential role in ensuring that international performances respect Malaysia’s laws and social harmony.
However, effective regulation in the digital age requires media literacy and a resistance to reactionary interpretations born out of viral, out-of-context video clips.

If Malaysia wishes to remain a premier destination for global live entertainment, bringing vital economic and tourism benefits to Kuala Lumpur, authorities must evaluate performances within their full artistic context.
Distinguishing between pop-culture symbolism and actual religious worship is not just good cultural policy; it is essential for fair and rational governance.
Jamaluddin Aziz is an FMT reader.

08367870b5ce119e: A series of tax cuts since President George W. Bush's 2001 legislation have helped push the national debt to US$32 trillion. AP Photo/Ron EdmondsDemocrats, set to take over Congress with robust majorities, will face at least one expensive obstacle to their policy agenda: a national debt that now equals the size of the U.S. economy. Clocking in at US$32 trillion, this debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% would likely raise alarms for other countries. But it attracted relatively little attention in an election season dominated by concerns over the economy and the cost of living. Debt has grown to these levels because over the past 25 years, the federal government has been spending more than it collects in taxes. Even as the U.S. economy grew, lawmakers have cut taxes repeatedly, sometimes with bipartisan support, instead of paying down debt. The series of tax cuts since 2001 has added over $10 trillion to the debt, according to an analysis of Congressional Budget Office data by the Center for American Progress. In fact, without these series of cuts, the debt-to-GDP ratio would be decreasing, the study found. The debate over taxation often falls along partisan lines, with arguments focusing on which income groups are affected or the potential impact on economic growth. But as a public policy scholar, I believe that important context is often overlooked. Under conditions of strong gross domestic product growth and low debt, tax cuts may have a relatively benign fiscal impact. But today, because debt as a share of GDP is so much higher, and interest rates are steeper, the cost of adding new debt is much greater than 15 or 20 years ago, whether through additional spending or through tax cuts. I believe Democrats will have to wrestle with this math as they try to advance a policy agenda focused on affordability that minimizes the risk of further borrowing. It’s all relative Proponents of fiscal austerity argue that lower spending should accompany tax cuts so that debt doesn’t rise. U.S. federal spending, however, has remained relatively flat – outside of emergencies like the 2009 recovery package and COVID-19 stimulus funds – even as GDP has risen. At the same time, each round of tax cuts over the past quarter century has actually gotten smaller over time if they’re assessed as a share of GDP, as a study by the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan think tank, noted. President Ronald Reagan’s 1981 tax cuts were the most expensive in history, reducing annual federal revenue on average by 2.9% of GDP, according to the Tax Foundation’s analysis. The next two biggest cuts occurred in 1945 and 1948, when the government rolled back the wartime hikes that helped pay for World War II. President Barack Obama’s 2012 legislation, extending most of the temporary tax cuts passed under President George W. Bush, comes in fourth at 1.8% of GDP, while cuts passed under President Lyndon Johnson in 1964 rank fifth. Coming in sixth place at 1.2% of GDP: President Donald Trump’s sweeping policy and tax legislation in 2025, which made permanent most of his 2017 tax cuts. Costly extensions While the Trump cuts amounted to a relatively small share of GDP, they had a much larger effect on the national debt due in part to the higher cost of borrowing. The original 2017 legislation was projected to increase public debt from 91.2% to 97.1% of GDP by 2027, with an overall 10-year cost of $1.5 trillion. That was based on the assumption the cuts would expire after 2025. But just like the earlier round of Bush tax cuts, Congress was loathe to let those provisions lapse. In 2025, the narrow Republican majority pushed through Trump’s legislation that extended or made permanent the 2017 cuts. The Congressional Budget Office, the independent government scorekeeper of legislation, estimated that the 2025 bill would add another $3.4 trillion over 10 years. And it projected that increasing deficits would push debt to 116% of GDP by the end of 2034. Why deficits and economic growth matter so much A basic calculation explains when debt stays stable, and when it does not. If a government runs a “primary” budget surplus – that is, excluding interest payments – and economic growth is higher than the interest rate on government bonds, debt remains stable. The problem for the U.S. is that budget deficits have been growing faster than the economy, while interest payments on government debt are rising as well. This math explains why the trajectory of economic growth is so important in understanding the impact of tax cuts. When taxes were cut after World War II, the economy was booming, the U.S. carried little debt, and reducing taxes didn’t further add to it. By contrast, government spending ballooned under Reagan, thanks in large part to defense outlays. Combined with lower tax revenue due to tax cuts, the national debt tripled during Reagan’s time in office. In 2000, the economy was surging again. That was the last time the U.S. took in more tax revenue than it spent and began paying down the debt. President George W. Bush cited this surplus to justify his first round of major tax cuts in 2001, which also drew support from some Democrats. It remains to be seen how much leverage the results of the midterms will grant Democratic lawmakers in the next two years as they try to enact legislation under Trump. But I believe lawmakers of all stripes will have to confront the hard choices that the U.S. national debt imposes on policy directions going ahead, thanks to a long series of decisions made over the past quarter century. 1b207d990733aaf1: Nearby stores might not actually win out with extra shoppers if a Walmart shutters. Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty ImagesShoppers often greet the closure of a Walmart with dismay, while competitors find cause to celebrate. Among critics of the big-box behemoth, a long-held assumption is that once a Walmart disappears, shoppers seeking groceries, household goods, meals and services will flow to businesses down the road. But what if the economic downside of a closure is bigger? We are marketing scholars who have studied dozens of Walmart closures in the United States. We found that nearby stores saw a slump in both monthly shopper traffic and sales revenue by roughly a quarter in contrast to comparable stores near Walmart locations that remained open. Our sample covered 39 Walmart stores that closed across 20 states from 2019 to 2026. This finding suggests a large retailer can play two roles at once. Walmart competes with neighboring businesses for shopper visits and spending. But it can also act as an anchor, giving people a reason to travel to a shopping area in the first place. When that anchor disappears, the loss of shared shopper traffic can outweigh the benefit of having one less competitor. The benefits of an anchor Our finding underscores that retailers don’t operate as isolated dots on a map. Shoppers often decide where to go before deciding which stores they’ll visit once they get there. A trip to Walmart can generate a stop at a nearby restaurant, pharmacy, salon, specialty retailer or service business. Economists call this kind of benefit an agglomeration effect: Businesses can gain from being near other businesses because the location itself attracts shoppers. Shopping center owners have long recognized this logic by using prominent stores to anchor a mix of tenants. Other researchers have found that Walmart’s entry into a shopping area causes sales in nearby existing stores to drop. But these shops can adjust their product assortment, prices and promotions to mitigate this effect, follow-up studies suggest. What has not been studied until now is what happens when a Walmart store – or any other anchor store – closes. A Walmart closure creates a tug-of-war between two forces, we argue. Competitive relief helps nearby businesses because a formidable rival is gone. But agglomeration loss hurts them because fewer shoppers have a reason to visit the area. This means a store can capture a larger share of local consumer demand after Walmart leaves and still end up worse off if the total pool of shoppers arriving in the area shrinks enough. Developers often place an anchor store in a bigger retail center to attract more foot traffic overall, which in turn goes to other stores. David Cooper/Toronto Star via Getty Images What happened after a Walmart closed We combined closure dates with monthly store-level shopper traffic and spending data. For each closed Walmart, we identified nearby non-Walmart businesses and compared their post-closure performance with that of businesses near Walmarts that stayed open. We discovered not just a sizable decline in both shopper traffic and sales revenue after closure but a worsening trend in both over time. Specifically, following a Walmart’s closure, nearby stores experienced a roughly 5% drop in the following month and 6% in the month thereafter. The decline keeps getting worse, reaching about 17% in the ninth month and 20% a year after the anchor store closes. That parallel movement in traffic and sales matters. If nearby stores were simply selling less to the same number of shoppers, we would expect spending per visit to fall. Instead, what was also happening is that fewer shoppers visited nearby businesses after the anchor disappeared. In short, competitive relief didn’t overcome the loss of traffic that would have been generated by trips to the anchor store. But not all nearby businesses were affected equally. Stores that competed more directly with Walmart had better post-closure sales than noncompeting stores. That is what we would expect if competitive relief is real: Grocery stores and other close substitutes are better positioned to capture some of the displaced consumer demand. Well-known brand stores also fared relatively better than unbranded businesses. A recognizable brand can give shoppers an independent reason to visit, reducing reliance on traffic generated by the nearby anchor. And stores surrounded by more outlets with its own brands also had more favorable post-closure sales. Another important factor is digital reach. Not surprisingly, the more a business engages with customers online, the less it depends on people physically traveling to a cluster of stores. We found that stores with a higher share of revenue from online orders saw a less severe drop in sales after a Walmart closed. These patterns suggest that managers have options and can act: Opening another location or expanding online sales can protect a retailer from an anchor closure. Why a store closing can become a neighborhood shock A large retailer decides whether to keep a store open based primarily on what makes sense for its own portfolio. But the surrounding businesses face a different calculation. A location that looks weak from the anchor retailer’s perspective can still drive valuable traffic to neighboring stores. That creates what economists call an externality – a positive or negative effect of an economic activity that impacts other parties even though market prices don’t reflect it. In this case, some of the economic value produced by an anchor sits outside the anchor’s own sales and profits. For neighboring businesses, the lesson is not to assume that a powerful competitor’s departure will create a windfall. Rather, managers need to know how many customers arrive because of the broader shopping destination, not merely how much their store’s products overlap with the anchor’s. Meanwhile, commercial property owners should treat losing an anchor as more than risking an empty storefront. It can also hurt the rest of their portfolio by reducing consumer demand. Replacing the tenant quickly matters, but so does finding a replacement that can generate trips to the area. Finally, local governments and economic development organizations need to understand that a major retail closure may affect businesses with no contractual relationship to the closed store. So their responses should extend beyond the vacant property itself – whether it’s speeding redevelopment, coordinating with local businesses and property owners to improve shoppers’ access, or helping create a new destination that restores shopper traffic. 4668ffcb5b4538a3: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible.

Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize.
Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations?

EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted:

“We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.”
A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem

As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on.
Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience.

That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions.
Beyond optimization

For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways.

The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential.

Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness.
Understanding traditional smelting vs. new proprietary technology

Development of the technology began in the United States in 2021 for chromite from Outokumpu’s Kemi mine in Finland, the only chrome mine in the European Union and one of the few such operations across the Western world. Since then, Outokumpu has evolved the technology through extensive research and development, combining new process chemistries with proprietary metallurgical expertise, supported in part by a non-exclusive patent license agreement from MIT.

“The technology is a new application for separating metallic elements from materials,” explains Allanore. Historically, that separation has been achieved using carbon- and energy-intensive approaches. The new method creates a different chemical environment that enables more efficient extraction with fewer losses and fewer unwanted by-products, recovering critical materials from resources considered waste.
Innovation happens at the boundaries

EvoMaterials sits at the intersection of several scientific disciplines, a combination that strongly resonates with Stinn, who completed his PhD in Materials Science and Engineering at MIT, where his research focused on low-carbon metals processing and recycling technologies.

Modern materials innovation draws on a growing mix of chemistry, materials science, physics, computational modeling, and engineering. With advanced simulation tools and AI helping researchers identify promising directions, scientific discovery still depends on experimentation and testing in the lab—on getting your hands dirty and doing the hard work.

“Science today is much more interdisciplinary than it was, and the collaboration across disciplines reveals new scientific opportunities,” says Stinn. Engineering can translate those opportunities into more efficient and cost-competitive metals production.
Building a technology platform

A technically significant aspect of EvoMaterials is that it’s not a single process, but a technology platform. Allanore compares EvoMaterials to platform technologies in other industries, where a single scientific breakthrough can enable multiple downstream applications.

Once a new extraction pathway has been mastered for one material system, the same scientific principles may be adapted to entirely different metals and mineral resources. The initial application becomes only the starting point.
“The future and the potential impact might be much broader than the original and current developments that are happening,” Allanore explains.
That possibility is increasingly important as industries seek secure supplies of nickel, chromium, molybdenum, and other strategic materials needed for advanced manufacturing.
The future of materials companies

The broader implication extends beyond metallurgy. Companies that develop proprietary process technologies may create value through production but also through intellectual property and scientific expertise.

Based on Outokumpu’s technology leadership, that transition could create entirely new categories of value, enabling the production of high-value critical materials from ores and resource streams that previously appeared uneconomical or inaccessible.

The result would be a fundamental shift in how metals are manufactured, where sustainability, resource efficiency, supply security, and economic value become outcomes of the same technological architecture rather than separate objectives.

The next step for EvoMaterials is pilot-scale validation, with a pilot plant in New Hampshire to begin operations in the first half of 2027. The facility will scale the proprietary technology from laboratory to one-ton production, providing a step toward industrial-scale deployment targeted for 2030. Beyond producing low-CO2, chromium-enriched ferrochrome and chromium metal, the platform could be adapted to other strategic materials, including nickel and molybdenum.
The work raises a broader question—how many of today’s metallurgical processes would look the same if they were invented from scratch? Or could those routes be designed differently today?
The next revolution in materials may begin by rethinking how to extract the metals that society depends on.

82fda640970b5538: Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting.

Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones.

Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider.

f60cbf1284a615ee: MIT researchers will lead an up to $53 million effort, awarded by the U.S. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) as part of its STREAM (Systems for Tracking and Resilience in Efficient Agricultural-input Management) program, to develop next-generation weed killers that help farmers and protect human health.  More than 1 billion pounds of herbicide are used in the United States every year. Herbicides help farmers by preventing significant crop loss due to weeds, and they enable regenerative farming practices that protect the soil, but some weeds are becoming resistant to the most common herbicides.  Exposure to herbicides may contribute to increased risk of cancer, metabolic and endocrine disorders, and other adverse health outcomes. Farm workers can be exposed from frequent herbicide use, but many U.S. residents are also exposed to these chemicals in small amounts through food and drinking water.  The MIT-led research team will develop new generative artificial intelligence tools to help them discover herbicide alternatives that are more effective and developed with human health in mind. Such alternatives could also help to reduce U.S. dependency on imported phosphorus, which is a critical ingredient in a major herbicide, glyphosate. “With herbicides like glyphosate and atrazine, there’s a real crisis because of resistance mutations that are coming,” says Christopher Voigt, head of MIT’s Department of Biological Engineering. “And if you combine the resistance mutations with issues around national security of the supply chain of the precursors to herbicides, we could find ourselves without these core agrochemicals that are absolutely essential for getting the high crop yields and economical prices that the United States now sees.” Voigt is the principal investigator for the project, known as Precision Learning for On-target Weed control (PLOW). The team is also expected to include researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the University of Tennessee at Knoxville, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, and Robigo. The researchers are grouped into three teams that will tackle different aspects of the project, aligned with the STREAM Technical Areas. The generative AI group will develop models that can predict molecules — either chemical compounds or small interfering RNA (siRNA) — that disrupt the same plant enzymes targeted by glyphosate and other herbicides. Glyphosate kills weeds by interfering with an enzyme called EPSP synthase, which plants need to produce several critical amino acids. After many years of herbicide use, some weeds have begun to acquire genetic mutations that allow them to become resistant to those herbicides, which makes them less effective and poses a significant threat to crop yields. “There’s a real need for new herbicides because of resistance mutations that have been arising,” Voigt says. “There are also concerns about herbicides’ possible impacts on the environment and on humans, so it’s important to identify alternative ways of making herbicides, which as a general class of molecule are really critical to agriculture.” The MIT-led team plans to design generative AI models that will be able to predict molecules that can help prevent resistance from arising. The models will also optimize for other features such as low cost of synthesis, low risk of inducing resistance, and low risk of harming humans or causing ecological damage.  The group developing these AI models is led by Connor Coley, the Warren K. Lewis Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering at MIT; Regina Barzilay, the School of Engineering Distinguished Professor for AI and Health at MIT; and Alexander Tropsha, the K.H. Lee Distinguished Professor in the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy. The models are expected to generate billions of possible candidates, which will then be tested by a second research team. This high-throughput screening group will be led by Angela Koehler, the Charles W. and Jennifer C. Johnson Professor of Biological Engineering at MIT, and Jaime Cheah, the associate director of scientific outreach and collaborative screening in the Center for the Development of Therapeutics at the Broad Institute. “Those libraries will be screened both to identify those molecules that hit their target, but also to then provide all of that screening data back to the computational approach in order to improve it,” Voigt says. Once the candidate pools are narrowed down, researchers on a third team will begin greenhouse studies to evaluate how each molecule performs under different agricultural conditions. That team will be led by Neal Stewart and Scott Lenaghan, co-directors of the Center for Agricultural Synthetic Biology at UTK; Patrick Tranel, the Tom and Peggy Ainsworth Professor of Crop Sciences at the University of Illinois; Tim Willson, the Harold Kohn Distinguished Professor at the UNC Eshelman School of Pharmacy; and Andee Wallace PhD ’20, CEO and founder of Robigo.  The first greenhouse tests of initial RNAi candidates are expected to be complete by the end of the first year of the program. As part of this project, the research team will also develop living microbial systems that degrade agrochemicals before they reach food, soil, or waterways. Engineered bacteria, fungi, and srRNA will convert chemicals and formulation ingredients into biomass, providing a scalable strategy to reduce environmental and human exposure. This research is funded by the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H) under agreement number 140D042690030. 548b35050a568476: The global race to build artificial intelligence (AI) data centres is entering a politically sensitive phase. Those in the United States just witnessed a massive electoral recoil. The Republican party was thrashed. Badly.
Hence, Malaysia must understand the implications before becoming an alternative destination for facilities facing growing resistance in the United States.
As they head to Malaysia, Putrajaya must understand these data centres come with huge political costs as President Donald Trump has discovered on Nov 3, 2026 in the mid-term election. Why?
For much of Trump’s second administration, the White House has encouraged American technology giants to accelerate investments in AI infrastructure.
The underlying assumption was straightforward.
Whoever controls the largest computing capacity will enjoy a decisive advantage in the development of advanced AI, including potentially super intelligent systems.
Yet technological ambition does not automatically translate into public acceptance.
Across the United States, opposition to hyperscale data centres has grown over electricity consumption, water requirements, noise pollution, land use and the possibility of higher utility bills.
These concerns have become politically significant.
Democratic politicians, including Gina Hinojosa in Texas, Amy Acton in Ohio and Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, have called for pauses on major data centre developments.
Democrats have also discussed congressional investigations into technology companies, raising the prospect of greater scrutiny over the environmental and economic consequences of AI expansion.
The significance extends beyond American domestic politics.
When the world’s largest AI market encounters resistance to physical infrastructure, international investors will reassess where future computing capacity can be built.
Malaysia is an obvious candidate for consideration. International trade and industry minister Johari Ghani is well aware of the risks based on his public statements though.
Malaysia’s geographical position, proximity to Singapore, expanding digital infrastructure and relative political stability make it attractive to multinational technology companies.
Johor has already emerged as a major data centre destination, while investments in Selangor and other states are expanding Malaysia’s digital footprint.

But Malaysia must distinguish between attracting high-quality digital investment and becoming a convenient location for infrastructure that other countries increasingly regard as environmentally burdensome.
A hyperscale data centre is not an ordinary manufacturing facility.
It can consume enormous amounts of electricity continuously, require substantial cooling infrastructure and place additional demands on water resources.
The economic benefits are also uneven.
Construction creates employment, but permanent staffing requirements can be relatively modest compared with the scale of capital invested.
Moreover, expensive imported semiconductor chips and specialised equipment may account for a substantial proportion of investment expenditure.
Malaysia therefore cannot assume that every billion-ringgit investment announced translates into an equivalent expansion of domestic technological capabilities.
The government must ask whether these investments strengthen Malaysia’s AI sovereignty or merely turn the country into a host for foreign-owned computing infrastructure.
This distinction is crucial.

If Malaysian electricity, water and land support AI systems whose intellectual property, strategic decisions and profits remain overwhelmingly overseas, the long-term national benefits may be limited.
Conversely, carefully negotiated investments could strengthen local research, engineering capabilities, cloud services, cybersecurity and the development of Malaysian AI models.
The difference lies in the conditions imposed before approval. Malaysia should require credible assessments of electricity demand, water consumption, grid capacity and environmental sustainability.

It should also establish transparent mechanisms to ensure that ordinary households and small businesses do not indirectly subsidise infrastructure used by exceptionally wealthy technology corporations.
Renewable energy commitments must be verifiable rather than promotional.
Equally important, data centre investments should generate meaningful technology transfers, skilled employment and opportunities for Malaysian universities and enterprises.
Malaysia must avoid repeating the familiar pattern of welcoming foreign capital without sufficiently strengthening domestic technological ownership.
There is also an Asean dimension.
Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam are competing to attract digital investments.
Competition without coordination could encourage governments to offer excessive incentives while overlooking environmental costs.
Asean should instead develop common principles governing sustainable AI infrastructure.
These could include energy efficiency, water security, cybersecurity, data protection and responsible management of increasingly autonomous AI systems.
Malaysia can contribute to such regional discussions while maintaining an investment environment that remains competitive.
The American backlash against hyperscale data centres is not necessarily a rejection of artificial intelligence itself.
It reflects a growing distinction between the benefits promised by AI and the physical costs imposed on communities hosting its infrastructure.
Malaysia should learn from that distinction.
The country needs foreign investment, but it also needs affordable electricity, reliable water supplies, environmental protection and technological independence.
These objectives are not mutually exclusive. They require disciplined planning and regulatory enforcement.
Malaysia should welcome AI investments that deepen its technological capabilities, not simply those seeking cheaper land, electricity and regulatory approval.
The United States is discovering that the infrastructure underpinning AI carries political and social costs.
Malaysia should not wait until those costs become domestic controversies before responding.
The next generation of AI data centres may indeed look increasingly towards Southeast Asia.
Malaysia must ensure that becoming a preferred destination does not mean inheriting problems that others have begun to resist.
Otherwise, the federal and state governments both risk a voters’ revolt as seen in the United States.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
42bc912dc85d4181: Seperti parti politik di mana-mana negara termasuklah Malaysia, mempunyai parti yang memperjuangkan berbagai ideologi. Dengan ideologi ini mereka mencari pengikut. Nasionalisme, sosialisme, sekularisme termasuklah membawa idealisme agama. Fahaman ini disebar kepada rakyat agar menyokong agenda mereka yang mereka percaya terbaik untuk semua.

Tetapi, dalam usaha mengekalkan sokongan, manipulasi tetap berlaku. Paling sedap guna agama. Alasan, dalil dan nas dipakai untuk mencari kelebihan ataupun menutup kelemahan sendiri. Pahala, dosa, syurga dan neraka dijadikan modal niaga untuk mengabsahkan tindakan mereka.

Seorang pemimpin politik sebuah parti agama dalam ceramahnya beberapa minggu lalu menjawab kritikan mengapa negeri yang ditadbir oleh mereka selama 36 tahun lambat maju dengan jawapan yang mudah. "Kita bukannya nabi." Senang, kan?

Pasti penyokong mereka terpesona dan kagum dengan jawapan itu. Tiada yang benar melainkan benar belaka hujah itu. Betullah tu, kita bukan nabi, kata penyokong mereka. Kita tak sempurna. Tetapi, bila kerajaan persekutuan atau kerajaan negeri lain yang ditadbir oleh musuh politik mereka lambat, dalam hal banjir di Selangor misalnya apa yang penyokong mereka tak hentam? Kenapa tak letak hujah pemimpin kamu itu kepada keadaan pihak lain?
"Benda bukan boleh selesai sehari dua, kita bukan nabi, kan?"

Terbaru, minggu lalu seorang lagi pemimpin parti itu dalam hantaran yang dibuatnya di Facebook menulis orang yang menderma untuk membantu bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak membayar denda RM50 juta boleh mendapat pahala. Beliau mengaitkan sumbangan itu dan segala bantuan berkaitan dengannya adalah usaha memudahkan urusan. Memudahkan urusan orang dapat pahala. Peh!

Kenyataan ini sangatlah menarik. Bukanlah sebab kita baru sahaja mengetahui bahawa menderma merupakan amalan yang baik dalam Islam. Sejak kecil kita sudah diajar begitu. Masukkan duit ke dalam tabung masjid, bantu anak yatim, beri makan orang miskin, semuanya amalan mulia. Tangan yang di atas lebih baik daripada tangan di bawah. Semua itu telah kita belajar.

Tetapi, apabila derma dikaitkan dengan seorang tokoh politik yang telah disabitkan kesalahan oleh mahkamah, persoalannya menjadi sedikit berbeza. Adakah setiap amalan derma yang kita buat kepada semua pihak itu sama nilainya? Itu yang lebai-lebai politik harus ajar pengikutnya. Selain nilai dan jumlah, perlu dididik juga tujuan sesuatu sumbangan itu apakah ia benar-benar dituntut dalam agama. Apakah ia membantu permasalahan ummah? Apakah akan memberi kebaikan dan keberkatan kepada bangsa, agama dan negara? Dari segi keadilan sejagat, apakah tindakan ini sesuai?

Maaflah, saya tak boleh terima bab seorang ahli politik merasakan dia ada autoriti untuk menentukan seseorang itu boleh mendapat pahala atau dosa. Kalau tolong pihak mereka, dapat pahala. Kalau buat perkara yang sama untuk pihak lain, berdosa. Sewaktu bermusuh habis semua pihak bergelumang dosa. Bila berbaik, kutip dalil untuk menyucikannya. Jika tempat orang ditimpa banjir itu murka Allah, jika tempat mereka kena, itu ujian. Ini amat memalukan jika kita fikir dengan akal yang waras. Saya mahu bertanya, ke mana penyokong kamu hendak dibawa? Barangkali ada segelintir penyokong parti kamu yang berasa malu juga dengan kenyataan ini.

Soal dosa pahala ini bukan perkara yang sedap-sedap jadi bahan mainan. Dalam kehidupan beragama, pahala dan dosa merupakan antara asas yang membentuk pertimbangan manusia. Orang melakukan kebaikan dengan mengharapkan ganjaran tuhan, manakala menjauhi kejahatan kerana takut akan balasan-Nya. Tapi mengapa bagi kamu, pahala dibuat seperti mata ganjaran untuk tebus barang di kedai serbaneka. Kita jadi ahli kedai, dapat kad keahlian, kemudian jika ada tawaran promosi, kita pun beli barang. Daripada pembelian barang, kita dapat 'point' (pahala) yang boleh ditebus kemudiannya. Macam itu? Gila betul.

Begini, biar saya jelaskan. Dalam isu duit denda Najib, saya boleh faham jika ada penyokongnya yang bersungguh-sungguh mahu membantu beliau. Dalam politik, kesetiaan atau ketaasuban bukan sesuatu yang pelik. Semua parti ada penyokong fanatik. Mereka akan bermati-matian mempertahankan pemimpin mereka. Dan dalam isu Najib ini, ada juga yang bersimpati terhadapnya dan ada juga yang mengenang jasa ketika beliau berkuasa lalu mereka pun menderma. Itu hak mereka. Pemimpin parti lain, jika kalah saman pun akan ada penyokong mereka yang bantu buat kutipan dana.

Tetapi, mengusik sentimen penyokong dengan mempergunakan ganjaran pahala ini agak teruk, bagi saya jika kita fikir dalam-dalam. Apakah boleh kita guna 'fatwa' yang sama untuk kutip derma dan permudahkan urusan ratusan bekas banduan yang sudah bebas supaya urusan mereka dipermudahkan? Mereka terpaksa bergelut kesusahan dalam mendapat pekerjaan. Di mana seruan buat pahala kamu? Apakah manusia seperti mereka tak berguna di mata kamu? Bukankah mereka juga berhak kembali ke pangkuan masyarakat untuk menyumbang bakti dan tenaga? Kenapa berpilih-pilih? Di mana keadilannya kalau begitu?

Di luar sana, berapa ramai orang yang memerlukan bantuan untuk membayar kos rawatan, membeli keperluan sekolah anak atau menyelesaikan hutang akibat kesempitan hidup? Berapa ramai rakyat memerlukan air bersih di rumah? Apa usaha dan inisiatif kamu untuk memudahkan urusan mereka? Takkan kepada marhaen asyik dijual pahala dan syurga sahaja demi nak menutup kemalasan kamu berkhidmat? Jika kamu sebagai pentadbir negeri bekerja keras memberikan kemudahan urusan rakyat di bawah kamu, bukankah kamu juga akan mendapat pahala yang besar? Tapi kamu berhelah, 'kita bukan nabi'. Ini sangat teruk!

Apabila seorang ahli politik memakai jubah dan kopiah bercakap tentang pahala, kenyataannya tentulah akan diterima oleh penyokong mereka. Apatah lagi seseorang ahli politik itu mempunyai latar belakang pendidikan agama atau berasal daripada keluarga ulama yang dihormati. Itu akan jadi lebih kuat.

Tetapi, ayuhlah berfikir secara realistik, kita memang tidak tahu apakah dapat pahala atau tidak jika seseorang itu menderma kepada Najib. Jika dapat pun kita tak tahu bagaimana bentuknya, besar mana atau apa rupanya. Itu bukan kita yang tentukan.

Pemimpin yang fatanah seharusnya lebih tahu memilih perkataan sesuai dalam menyampaikan maksudnya. Tetapi, dek kerana miskin kata-kata dan hujah, maka modal niaga paling sesuai ialah menjual agama dan meletakkan pahala di atas meja. Apakah ahli politik merasakan bahawa tuhan memberikan mereka kuasa juga dalam mengagih pahala?
"Kepada sesiapa yang hendak menderma kepada Najib, dibolehkan kerana itu hak anda. Bersimpati, menolong dan memudahkan urusan orang lain adalah amalan yang digalakkan."
Hah! Saya rasa ayat sebegitu sudah cukup. Nampaklah bijak tanpa menanggalkan ciri ‘keustazannya’, kan?

Dalam sinis, saya tetap menganggap menjual pahala dan dosa dalam permainan politik adalah menghina kebijaksanaan rakyat. Kalau ahli politik pun boleh menentukan siapa dapat pahala, alamatnya selepas ini manifesto pilihan raya mungkin tidak lagi menjanjikan pembangunan, pekerjaan atau kos sara hidup yang lebih rendah. Cukuplah dengan janji pahala atau menggunakan alasan 'kita bukan nabi' seperti alasan seorang lagi pemimpin politik parti yang sama.
Malulah sikit. Kalau tak malu dengan tuhan, malulah sikit dengan segelintir penyokong parti kamu sendiri yang lebih bijak daripada kamu. Takkan kamu nampak mereka semua lekeh daripada kamu?

efe06b263df6f729: What do discarded batteries from BMW electric vehicles, second-life solar panels and an Orang Asli village deep in the jungles of Pahang have in common? Quite a lot, as I discovered at Kampung Saweh, Pos Sinderut, reached by a 70km jungle trail that takes about two hours to negotiate.

We had volunteered our 4WD vehicles to transport a Universiti Malaya team to the village. This mission was particularly interesting because it combined rural electrification, renewable energy and the reuse of electric vehicle batteries.

As a veteran off-roader, I've spent decades exploring jungle trails and enjoying camping by rivers. These days, one of the more satisfying uses of our 4x4 vehicles is transporting volunteers and equipment to marginalised rural communities.

Leading the project was Tan Chia Kwang, an associate professor, supported by 14 graduate and undergraduate students. The project received funding from Universiti Malaya's community engagement arm, and Ritsumeikan University of Japan, through Shoki Kosai, who is also an associate professor and partner in environmental research.
The initiative brought together academia, industry, and local communities to advance sustainable energy solutions for rural electrification.
Tan had already transported second-life solar panels, electrical wiring, ducts and timber for the Orang Asli villagers to construct solar panel racks and a battery house at Kampung Saweh.

The second-life solar panels were donated by Tech Inspiration Systems, and the students tested them to select healthy units capable of generating upwards of 280 Watts each. But solar panels alone cannot provide reliable electricity after sunset. That's where the battery energy storage system (BESS) comes in.

The battery modules were provided by BMW Malaysia as part of its support for the project, demonstrating the potential of second-life EV battery applications beyond automotive use. These are nickel-cobalt-manganese EV battery modules recovered from warranty replacements.
"I wrote to EV companies in Malaysia seeking partnership for our project. BMW responded and after numerous meetings agreed to support our project,” said Tan.
What the UM team did

Tan explained that his team developed proprietary technology for the project at the smart grid research laboratory of Universiti Malaya's power energy dedicated advanced centre, testing and repurposing battery components before transporting them into the Pahang jungle.
The energy centre, established in 2000, focuses on renewable energy, power electronics, energy storage, smart grids and related technologies.

“The team has developed proprietary technology for this BESS project, with students working late into the night in the lab testing and repurposing battery components before transporting them into the jungle.”

The actual installation was another challenge. Over an intense five days and four nights, the team worked to integrate the solar panels, electrical controls and 30 battery modules. They had to cook their own food -- instant noodles for most of them -- and sleep on the cold floor of the community hall.

The most time-consuming task was wiring the battery modules in what Tan called the "battery house" — a low-carbon bamboo hut built by the villagers. There was something rather appealing about this contrast: sophisticated batteries that once powered premium German EVs now housed in a traditional bamboo structure in the Pahang jungle.
A chance to watch TV

The system will serve 20 Orang Asli households, with each household allocated around 3kWh daily. This allocation is sufficient based on Tan's prior research into rural households’ electricity usage behaviour; Tan has more than 10 years of experience in rural electrification projects.

He said that one of the most important factors for a successful adoption of a battery storage system was engagement with the community. “Over the years, I’ve learnt that it needs several meetings with a Tok Batin and the community to gauge their commitment or adopt another kampung. We’ve been fortunate with this settlement. They’ve contributed more than I expected.”
And what were the villagers most excited about? The opportunity to watch Malaysia's national television channels at night!
It was a reminder that what urban Malaysians take for granted can be a major improvement in the quality of life for isolated rural communities.

However, a standalone solar-battery system cannot provide unlimited electricity supply. Tan has asked the connected households to keep their nightly consumption within an agreed limit, so that the stored energy can not only last through the night but also allow the batteries to achieve their projected lifespan of many years.
There is a bigger story here for Malaysia's rapidly growing EV industry.
Making recycling work

Many EV batteries retain substantial storage capacity even after they are no longer suitable for automotive use. As the data from the US indicates, most have demonstrated around 70% remaining state of health after prolonged service of up to 20 years, although this varies considerably.
Repurposing suitable batteries for stationary energy storage could extend their useful lives by years.

Tan also highlighted a weakness in Malaysia's recycling ecosystem. Some scrap dealers, he said, purchased discarded EV batteries under the mistaken impression that their weight indicated large quantities of valuable recyclable metal.

There are only four companies in Malaysia that are licensed to recycle EV batteries now. Unlike Europe, which is introducing battery passports to improve traceability, Malaysia has yet to establish a comparable comprehensive system.
The Kampung Saweh project demonstrates how properly tested second-life EV batteries can provide useful energy storage instead of prematurely entering the waste stream.

For our volunteer 4x4 transporters from the Land Rover Exchange community, the expedition was another reminder that off-roading needn't be just about adventure. Sometimes, the most satisfying destination is a remote village where a little goodwill, university ingenuity and discarded EV batteries can bring something as simple — and meaningful — as television after sunset.
